question:
A 33-year-old female presents 6 weeks after the birth of her first child with a two-week history of polyarthralgia, fever and a skin rash. First-line investigations show:


ESR	45 mm/hour

What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which one of the following is least associated with Behcet's syndrome?
explanation:
Oral ulcers + genital ulcers + anterior uveitis = Behcet's

Mouth ulcers, genital ulcers, deep vein thrombosis and aseptic meningitis are all recognised features of Behcet's syndrome

Ocular involvement is the most feared complication of Behcet's syndrome. Conjunctivitis is seen rarely and is much less common than anterior uveitis. Other ocular problems seen include retinal vasculitis, iridocyclitis and chorioretinitis

question:
A 52-year-old male presents with a four-month history of joint pain.

His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes and hypothyroidism, and he is hard of hearing. He recently attended with carpal tunnel syndrome. He reports his father having had bone problems too.

Examination is grossly unremarkable other than some limitation in range of movement due to pain in several joints, and visible scoliosis. There is no deformity of any visible bone.

Some of his blood results are reported below:


Calcium	2.3 mmol/L	(2.1 - 2.6)
Phosphate	0.9 mmol/L	(0.8 - 1.4)
Vitamin D	30 ng/ml	(20 - 50)
Urea	4.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	63 µmol/L	(55 - 120)


Bilirubin	5 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	42 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	20 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	8 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	40 g/L	(35 - 50)

What is the single most fitting diagnosis?
explanation:
Patients with osteopetrosis have normal calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH levels

Osteopetrosis, or marble bone disease, is a rare condition characterised by bone hardening due to the malfunction of osteoclasts. Paradoxically, this can still lead to an increased risk of fractures. Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis (ADO) is also known as Albers-Schonberg disease and is the most likely diagnosis here, in view of his father having had similar problems. Normal blood results, bone pain, and nerve compression (carpal tunnel and sensorineural hearing loss are both quite common in osteopetrosis) are all features of this condition. Scoliosis is another common feature, and in some patients, it is the only manifestation. Phosphate is typically normal in type I ADO, but it can be very high in type II ADO, which also carries a higher risk of fractures.

Osteoporosis would also present with normal blood tests but is less likely to cause neurological symptoms (carpal tunnel, hearing loss) and is not autosomal dominant. It would also not cause scoliosis.  Whilst it is much more common than osteopetrosis, and in real life may still be the most 'likely' diagnosis statistically speaking, it is not the most 'fitting' diagnosis when compared to osteopetrosis.

Paget's disease would likely cause a rise in ALP, at least in an exam setting. It is a very valid differential in this case as the presentation can be similar, and it may also cause sensorineural hearing loss due to compression at the skull level. However, it would more typically present with bone deformity (absent in this case), and it wouldn't be as likely to cause scoliosis.

Osteomalacia (low vitamin D in adults) would cause low calcium, low phosphate, high ALP and high PTH. This patient has normal blood results.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism is typically seen in chronic kidney failure as a response to low calcium due to kidneys failing to convert vitamin D into its active form. Bloods would show a low vitamin D, low or normal calcium, and of course, a high PTH. There is no mention of the patient having renal disease.

question:
A 28-year-old man has 2 days of a painful, red left eye and blurred vision. His left eye shows conjunctival injection, ciliary flush, an irregular pupil, and hypopyon.

His past medical history includes an episode of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea 6 months ago, with endoscopy showing ileal ulcers. He also has intermittent joint pain that improves with exertion, recurrent mouth ulcers, a prior episode of genital ulcers unresponsive to aciclovir, and painful nodules on his shins.

Which antigen is most likely to be present in this patient?
explanation:
Behcet's syndrome is associated with HLA B51

HLA-B51

is correct. The most likely diagnosis is Behçet’s syndrome, given the presence of anterior uveitis with ciliary flush, hypopyon, painful red eye, and an irregular pupil, alongside recurrent oral and genital ulcers, erythema nodosum (painful nodules on the shins), intermittent arthritis, and ileal ulcers causing abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. This multisystem involvement, mucocutaneous, ocular, gastrointestinal, and articular, is characteristic of Behçet’s syndrome. HLA-B51 is strongly associated with Behçet’s, especially in populations from the Mediterranean and East Asia. Although not diagnostic, its presence increases susceptibility and supports the diagnosis when clinical features are compatible.

HLA-A3

is incorrect because it is associated with hereditary haemochromatosis, which typically presents with iron overload features such as fatigue, arthralgia, and liver dysfunction. It does not cause recurrent oral and genital ulcers, anterior uveitis with hypopyon, or ileal ulceration. These features are consistent with Behçet’s syndrome, which is instead associated with HLA-B51.

HLA-B27

is incorrect. Although this is associated with anterior uveitis, this would occur without the mouth, genital, and gastrointestinal ulceration seen in this patient. HLA-B27 is also more commonly linked to seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis. These conditions typically present with inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis, and enthesitis, not with recurrent oral and genital ulcers, erythema nodosum, or ileal ulceration. Reactive arthritis may cause conjunctivitis and urethritis but lacks the multisystem vasculitis and mucocutaneous involvement typical of Behçet’s syndrome.

HLA-DR3

is incorrect because it is associated with autoimmune conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  MS presents with optic neuritis, motor and sensory deficits, and relapsing-remitting neurological symptoms, while SLE manifests with malar rash, joint pain, renal involvement, and haematological abnormalities. This patient's oral and genital ulcers, anterior uveitis with hypopyon, erythema nodosum, or ileal ulcers are more in keeping with Behçet’s syndrome, which is linked to HLA-B51.

HLA-DR4

is incorrect because it is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes.  RA presents with symmetric joint swelling, prolonged morning stiffness, and rheumatoid nodules, whereas type 1 diabetes causes polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight loss. In contrast, this patient’s oral and genital ulcers, anterior uveitis with hypopyon, erythema nodosum, or ileal ulcers point to Behçet’s syndrome, which is a multisystem vasculitis associated with HLA-B51.

question: A 28-year-old man is diagnosed with having ankylosing spondylitis. He presented with a six month history of back pain. On examination there is reduced lateral flexion of the spine but no evidence of any other complications. Which one of the following is he most likely to offered as first-line treatment?
explanation:
Exercise regimes and NSAIDs are the 1st line management for ankylosing spondylitis

The anti-TNF drugs are currently only used for patients with severe ankylosing spondylitis which has failed to respond to NSAIDs.

question: Stephen is a 57-year-old man who has late ankylosing spondylitis. What pulmonary feature might you see on his chest radiograph?
explanation:
May be able to see apical fibrosis on chest x-ray in later ankylosing spondylitis

You may be able to see apical fibrosis on chest x-ray in later ankylosing spondylitis.

Peripheral granulomas form after inflammation. Causes include infection, TB and sarcoidosis.

Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is often related to sarcoidosis and possibly lymphoma.

Increased pulmonary vasculature markings can be related to congestion or pulmonary hypertension.

question:
A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a painful swollen wrist. She is currently on oral antibiotics for a urinary tract infection. She has a past medical history of osteoarthritis.

Observations:


Heart rate 88 beats per minute
Blood pressure 145/75 mmHg
Respiratory rate 18/minute
Oxygen saturations 96% on room air
Temperature 37.1C

On examination, the left wrist is erythematous, tender and swollen with a restricted range of motion.

Plain radiography of the left wrist reveals calcification of the triangular fibrocartilage.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chondrocalcinosis helps to distinguish pseudogout from gout

Pseudogout

is the correct answer. The patient presents with a monoarthritis of the left wrist. The most common causes of monoarthritis are septic arthritis and crystal arthritis. However, crystal arthritis is far more common than native joint septic arthritis. Calcification of the triangular fibrocartilage suggests chondrocalcinosis. This occurs in pseudogout but is not associated with gout. Flares of pseudogout are common in those patients with intercurrent infection. Age, sex and osteoarthritis are also risk factors for this condition and the wrist is commonly affected. While pseudogout is the most likely diagnosis, the joint should still be aspirated to exclude infection. The mortality of septic arthritis is almost 10% and it is an important diagnosis not to miss.

Gout

is incorrect. This is another plausible cause of monoarthritis. However, the radiological findings in this case (and the joint affected) favour pseudogout rather than gout.

Psoriatic arthritis

is incorrect. Any inflammatory arthritis can theoretically present as monoarthritis. However, it is more typical for this type of inflammatory arthritis to present in an oligoarticular or polyarticular fashion. There may also be a family history or associated with a psoriatic rash. The plain x-ray may demonstrate juxta-articular new bone formation.

Rheumatoid arthritis

is incorrect. Any inflammatory arthritis can theoretically present as monoarthritis. However, it is more common for this type of inflammatory arthritis to present with small joint polyarthritis affecting the hands and feet. The plain x-ray may demonstrate erosions and juxta-articular osteopenia.

Septic arthritis

is incorrect. This is the most important diagnosis to exclude and all monoarthritis should be aspirated to exclude infection. A pre-existing infection (e.g. a UTI) is a risk factor. However, it is not the most likely diagnosis. Crystal arthritis is far more common than septic arthritis.

question:
A 34-year-old patient is referred for investigation of recurrent miscarriages. She has had four miscarriages in the first trimester of pregnancy. She does not have any children. She has a past medical history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and is on hydroxychloroquine.

Physical examination is unremarkable.

What blood test is most likely to support the underlying cause?
explanation:
SLE, recurrent miscarriages → check for antiphospholipid antibodies

Beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies

is the correct answer. The patient has a background of SLE. This is associated with secondary antiphospholipid syndrome which can cause recurrent miscarriages. There are three antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, beta-2 glycoprotein antibody, and cardiolipin antibody). Therefore, from the listed options. beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies are the correct answer.

Anti-Ro antibodies

is incorrect. This antibody may be positive in SLE but is more closely associated with Sjogren's syndrome. The significance in pregnancy is that children of mothers with anti-Ro antibodies are at risk of developing neonatal heart block. It is not a cause of recurrent miscarriage and so this is incorrect.

Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies

is incorrect. This antibody is associated with disease activity in SLE. However, it is not associated with recurrent miscarriage.

Beta-2 microglobulin antibodies

is incorrect. This is used as a prognostic marker in multiple myeloma and as a measure of disease activity. It is not associated with SLE or recurrent miscarriages.

Factor V Leiden gene analysis

is incorrect. Patients with the factor V Leiden gene mutation are at higher risk of thrombosis. There is data to suggest that there is an increased risk of miscarriage with this disorder. However, this is not classically associated with SLE and therefore beta-2 glycoprotein antibody testing is the correct answer.

question:
A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a swollen and painful left knee, as well as redness in both eyes. He also reports painful urination for two weeks, for which he has not sought medical attention. There is no history of back pain or trauma. He is sexually active with multiple partners.

On examination, his conjunctivae are injected, and his left knee is warm and swollen. Joint aspiration shows no organisms.

What will support the suspected diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
Urethritis + arthritis +/- conjunctivitis = reactive arthritis

Positive HLA-B27

is correct. This patient presents with the classic triad of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and asymmetric oligoarthritis, strongly suggesting reactive arthritis. HLA-B27 is present in a large proportion of patients with reactive arthritis and increases the likelihood that an acute post-infectious arthritis is part of the seronegative spondyloarthropathy spectrum. In this scenario, the patient’s recent genitourinary infection (painful urination, multiple sexual partners) and sterile joint aspirate make HLA-B27 positivity the most specific laboratory finding supporting the diagnosis.

Elevated C-reactive protein

is incorrect. CRP is a nonspecific marker of inflammation and can be elevated in many conditions, including infection, autoimmune arthritis, and trauma. Although it may be raised in reactive arthritis, it does not distinguish it from other causes of arthritis and is less supportive than HLA-B27 in this patient.

Positive ANA test

is incorrect. ANA positivity is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune diseases, which typically present with multisystem involvement (skin rash, nephritis, hematologic abnormalities). This patient lacks these features, so ANA does not strongly support reactive arthritis in this context.

Positive anti-CCP antibodies

is incorrect. Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, which typically presents as chronic, symmetric small joint polyarthritis. The patient’s acute, asymmetric knee arthritis, sterile synovial fluid, conjunctivitis, and urethritis make RA unlikely.

Positive rheumatoid factor

is incorrect. Rheumatoid factor is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, usually presenting as chronic, symmetric small joint involvement. This patient’s acute asymmetric arthritis and extra-articular features are inconsistent with RA, so a positive RF would not strongly support reactive arthritis.

question:
A 48-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 6-month history of joint pain and stiffness, especially in her wrists and small joints of her hands. She reports morning stiffness lasting over an hour and persistent fatigue.

On examination, her joints are swollen, warm, and tender. This is evidence of hyperextension of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints and flexion of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. X-rays show joint space narrowing and early erosions in the hand joints.

What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis: initial management is conventional DMARD monotherapy (usually methotrexate), often with short-term bridging corticosteroid

The most likely diagnosis is rheumatoid arthritis (RA), particularly in a 48-year-old woman, as she presents with joint pain and stiffness in the wrists and small joints, along with prolonged morning stiffness lasting over an hour. Clinical examination reveals swollen, warm joints with characteristic swan-neck deformity, which consists of hyperextension at the PIP joints and flexion at the DIP joints—a classical sign of RA. Radiographs demonstrating joint space narrowing and erosions are also commonly observed in RA.  Additionally, her persistent fatigue is consistent with the systemic symptoms frequently associated with this condition.

Methotrexate with short-term bridging corticosteroids

represents the correct initial management approach. Methotrexate is the first-line DMARD for RA, aiming to slow disease progression and prevent joint damage, while corticosteroids provide immediate symptomatic relief during the period required for methotrexate to exert its full effect.

Infliximab with NSAIDs

is not typically utilised as first-line therapy in RA. These agents are generally reserved for patients with an inadequate response to at least two conventional DMARDs including methotrexate or those presenting with severe disease activity.

Corticosteroids with NSAIDs

are not recommended for long-term management of RA. Although they effectively reduce inflammation and control symptoms rapidly, their use is usually limited to short-term relief—often serving as 'bridging' therapy while awaiting the onset of action from DMARDs such as methotrexate. Long-term corticosteroid use carries significant risks including osteoporosis, weight gain, and increased susceptibility to infections; furthermore, chronic concurrent administration of corticosteroids and NSAIDs heightens the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding among other complications.

Hydroxychloroquine

is indeed a DMARD employed in treating RA; however, it typically does not suffice as monotherapy for initial management. It may be used concomitantly with other DMARDs like methotrexate in more severe cases or when milder forms of RA are being treated. Hydroxychloroquine can serve as an adjunctive treatment but for initial management purposes, a combination of methotrexate and short-term corticosteroids is preferred due to their ability to more swiftly control inflammation and prevent joint damage.

NSAIDs with paracetamol

do not represent optimal initial management for a patient presenting with RA. While NSAIDs and paracetamol may alleviate pain and inflammation symptoms, they fail to modify the underlying disease process or forestall joint destruction. Initial treatment protocols typically involve DMARDs such as methotrexate that aim to retard disease progression and mitigate long-term articular damage. NSAIDs and paracetamol might be utilised adjunctively but are insufficient on their own as comprehensive treatment strategies for effectively managing RA.

question:
A 38-year-old man presents to the hospital with a one-week history of pain and stiffness in all of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of his left hand. He also reports stiffness in his neck and upper back. Otherwise, he feels systemically well and has not had any previous joint issues. The patient denies preceding trauma.

On examination of the patient's left hand, all the DIP joints are stiff and swollen, and the fourth finger is swollen. He has mild stiffness in his neck with a very slight reduction in cervical spine mobility. There are no other joint or skin abnormalities.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Inflammatory arthritis involving DIP swelling and dactylitis points to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis

Psoriatic arthritis

is the correct answer. Dactylitis and DIP swelling are characteristic changes of psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis can cause spinal stiffness and reduced cervical spine mobility. Note a patient can have psoriatic arthritis without having psoriatic skin changes.

Ankylosing spondylitis

is the incorrect answer. Ankylosing spondylitis does not present with changes to the joints in the hand.

Osteoarthritis

is the incorrect answer. The description of stiff and swollen joints is more in keeping with inflammatory arthritis. Additionally, osteoarthritis tends to affect larger joints and is very unlikely to present in someone of this age.

Reactive arthritis

is the incorrect answer. Reactive arthritis tends to occur after an infection elsewhere in the body. There is no evidence of this in this case.

Rheumatoid arthritis

is the incorrect answer. Rheumatoid arthritis more commonly affects the proximal interphalangeal joints as opposed to the DIP joints. Additionally, rheumatoid arthritis tends to be symmetrical, which is not the case in this patient.

question:
A 55-year-old right-handed male cleaner presents with elbow pain. He describes a gradual onset of pain in his right elbow over a period of six weeks with only mild relief from paracetamol. The patient plays golf and exercises at the gym weekly. He does remember a fall at work six weeks ago where he fell onto his left elbow. The patient feels systemically well and denies any pyrexia. On examination, the patient describes tenderness over the right elbow with resisted wrist extension/ supination and the elbow held in extension. There is no significant swelling over the olecranon.

What is the most likely cause of this man's elbow pain?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis: worse on resisted wrist extension/suppination whilst elbow extended

The most likely answer here is lateral epicondylitis. Lateral epicondylitis or 'tennis elbow' presents with gradual onset pain around the lateral epicondyle of the humerus radiating to the forearm. This patient's job is a cleaner, therefore undertaking repetitive movements with his dominant hand increases the chance of lateral epicondylitis.

Medial epicondylitis or 'golfer's elbow' presents with pain around the medial epicondyle. Pain is elicited during wrist flexion and pronation and does not match the examination findings in the scenario.

Olecranon bursitis presents with swelling and erythema over the olecranon, this patient does not have this as outlined in the question.

Radial head fractures present with immediate pain and swelling, the patient in this case presented with gradual onset pain; making a fracture a less likely differential in this patient.

As this patient is systemically well, septic arthritis is unlikely. Also, the affected joint will appear red, painful and swollen.

question: Each one of the following is seen in reactive arthritis, except:

A 53-year-old woman, who works as a ballet instructor, presents to her general practitioner with a 3-month history of progressively worsening pain in her right knee. She describes the pain as a dull ache that intensifies during her teaching sessions. Despite using hot packs for relief, she has found them ineffective.

On examination, there is a reduced range of motion and crepitus in the right knee. An X-ray shows the presence of osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis in the medial compartment of the knee.

What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment for her condition?
explanation:
Knee osteoarthritis - topical NSAIDs are first-line

Topical diclofenac

is correct. This woman has localised knee osteoarthritis, causing pain that worsens during ballet teaching. NICE recommends topical NSAIDs as first-line analgesics for knee or hand osteoarthritis. They provide effective local relief with fewer systemic risks. For someone needing to stay active professionally, avoiding side effects is important. The knee is also accessible for topical application.

Glucosamine supplement

is incorrect because NICE does not recommend glucosamine due to inconsistent evidence of benefit. It lacks anti-inflammatory or proven analgesic effects. In a physically active patient with functional limitations, relying on this could delay effective treatment. It would not address the patient’s worsening pain during activity.

Intra-articular corticosteroid

is incorrect because corticosteroid injections are generally used for acute flares or when standard treatments fail. This patient has chronic, stable pain with no effusion or signs of inflammation. Topical NSAIDs are safer and more appropriate as initial therapy. Steroids would not be the first choice in this case.

Oral ibuprofen

is incorrect because while effective, oral NSAIDs carry risks like gastrointestinal bleeding and kidney impairment. This patient presents with isolated knee pain and no contraindications to topical therapy. For someone with a physically demanding job, topical NSAIDs offer similar benefits with lower systemic risk. They are preferred for first-line use.

Paracetamol

is incorrect because NICE no longer recommends paracetamol as a preferred option due to limited effectiveness. It may be considered if NSAIDs are contraindicated, but this is not the case here. This patient has activity-related pain needing more effective relief. Topical NSAIDs are more suitable for her presentation.

question:
A 72-year-old man presents with right knee pain, vomiting, and rigors that have persisted for one week and have not improved with oral co-amoxiclav. He has a past medical history including hypertension, type two diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3.

His medication history includes ramipril, bendroflumethiazide, and dapagliflozin.

His temperature is 38.8ºC, and his blood pressure is 103/72 mmHg. Physical examination reveals a right knee effusion and reduced range of motion.

A joint aspirate shows purulent fluid and polymorphs but no identifiable organisms.

What treatment should be initiated?
explanation:
Gram staining is negative in around 30-50% of cases of septic arthritis

This patient is presenting with sepsis secondary to right knee septic arthritis. A negative gram stain does not exclude the diagnosis of septic arthritis, as the gram stain may be negative due to antibiotics administered in the community. The appropriate treatment is

IV flucloxacillin

, which is the treatment of choice for native joint septic arthritis because the causative organism is most likely

Staphylococcus aureus

.

Allopurinol

is used as a preventive treatment for gout. While gout should be considered in the differential diagnosis of acute synovitis, patients with gout typically do not present with septic symptoms and urate crystals would be expected in the joint aspirate. Risk factors for gout include CKD and diuretic use. Management of acute gout is supportive, with analgesia, and allopurinol is used to prevent recurrent attacks by lowering urate levels.

IM methotrexate

is a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug used primarily for inflammatory arthritis. Patients typically present with polyarthropathy and profound morning stiffness that improves throughout the day, although mono-articular presentations can occur. Methotrexate is likely to be harmful in this case due to its immunosuppressive effects.

Colchicine

is commonly used to treat acute gout but has no role in septic arthritis.

Rest, ice, compression and elevation

would be an inappropriate treatment choice for a patient with clinical septic arthritis which has been confirmed by joint aspiration. This would be an appropriate treatment for soft tissue injuries where there is no orthopaedic input required.

question:
A 48-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of symmetrical joint pain, stiffness, and swelling, primarily affecting her hands and wrists. She reports moderate morning stiffness lasting over an hour and fatigue.

Investigations:


anti-CCP	24 U/mL	(< 7)
ESR	50 mm/hr	(< 10)
CRP	25 mg/L	(< 5)

What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis: initial management is conventional DMARD monotherapy (usually methotrexate), often with short-term bridging corticosteroid

Methotrexate with prednisolone

is the correct answer. Methotrexate is the cornerstone of initial treatment for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) due to its potent anti-inflammatory and disease-modifying effects. It inhibits folate metabolism, thereby suppressing immune system overactivity that contributes to joint inflammation and damage. Starting methotrexate early helps to achieve remission or low disease activity, thereby preserving joint function and improving long-term outcomes in RA. The addition of a short-term corticosteroid like prednisolone provides rapid relief from symptoms whilst methotrexate's effects build up, helping to manage acute inflammation and pain effectively.

Hydroxychloroquine with prednisolone

is incorrect. Hydroxychloroquine is used in the treatment of RA, particularly in milder cases, as part of combination therapy, or when there are contraindications to the usage of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). However, it is generally not as effective as methotrexate in achieving disease control. Combining it with prednisolone therefore does not align with the standard initial management strategy for more severe RA.

Methotrexate with adalimumab

is incorrect. Although adalimumab, a TNF inhibitor, can be effective for RA, it is typically reserved for patients who do not respond to initial DMARD therapy. Starting with methotrexate alone, often with short-term corticosteroids, is the recommended initial approach.

Methotrexate with naproxen

is incorrect. Naproxen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug used to manage pain and inflammation in RA but does not have disease-modifying properties. Whilst it can be used for symptom relief, it does not replace the need for DMARDs like methotrexate, which address the underlying disease process.

Sulfasalazine with prednisolone

is incorrect. Sulfasalazine is another DMARD used to treat RA and can be part of initial therapy. However, methotrexate remains the preferred first-line DMARD due to its superior efficacy. Combining sulfasalazine with prednisolone is not typically the first choice for the initial treatment of RA.

question:
A 48-year-old man presents following a recurred episode of back pain. The patient has had multiple issues following a disc prolapse sustained during his career working in manual labour. The patient reports today he was bending over to pick something up and had an acute onset of lower back pain.

On exam, he had a unilateral, decreased sensation on the posterolateral aspect of the right leg and lateral foot. A straight leg raise test results in pain in the thigh, buttock and calf region and there is weakness on plantar flexion with reduced ankle reflexes.

What root compression has this patient experienced?
explanation:
S1 lesion features = Sensory loss of posterolateral aspect of leg and lateral aspect of foot,  weakness in plantar flexion of foot, reduced ankle reflex, positive sciatic nerve stretch test

This patient has presented with a prolapsed spinal disc producing an

S1 nerve root compression

. Disc prolapses normal produce a clear dermatomal pain pattern and neurological deficit due to a single nerve root being compressed. As seen in this case compression of the S1 nerve root results in a sensory loss of the posterolateral aspect of the leg and lateral aspect of the foot. There is a weakness of foot plantar flexion and ankle reflexes are normally reduced. Finally, pain can be elicited when the patient performs a straight leg raise; known as the sciatic nerve stretch test.

An

L1-2 nerve root compression

will result in discomfort over the groin and upper thigh region with associated weakness of the pelvic and psoas muscles. Although rare, patients suffering prolapse of the L1-2 discs often have difficulty lifting the affected leg and therefore struggle to walk upstairs etc.

The pain pattern and neurological deficit of an

L3 nerve root compression

is commonly a sensory loss over the anterior aspect of the thigh, weakness of the quadriceps with a reduction in the knee reflex on the affected side. Finally, pain can be elicited in the anterior thigh when performing the femoral stretch test, where the knee is passively flexed with the patient lying prone.

An

L4 nerve root compression

can present with a very similar pattern to an L3 compression with weakness of the quadriceps, a reduced knee reflex and a positive femoral stretch test. In L4 root compression, however, there will be a sensory loss over the anterior aspect of the knee, not the thigh.

L5 nerve root compression

can be identified on examination by evidence of sensory loss on the dorsum aspect of the foot with weakness of the foot and big toe dorsiflexion. L5 nerve compressions will also result in a positive sciatic nerve stretch test but the reflexes are normally unaffected.

question:
A 65-year-old woman presents to her GP with back pain and a history of frequent falls. She reports a family history of osteoporosis and is an ex-smoker.

Following a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan, her results indicate a T-score of -2.5 at the lumbar spine and hip, leading to a recommendation for bisphosphonate therapy.

Which population is her test score compared against?
options: Average bone mass of a population of the same age and sex
Average bone mass of a population with similar medical conditions
Bone mass of patients with a known history of osteoporosis
Bone mass of young adults of the same sex
correctText: Bone mass of young adults of the same sex
explanation:
DEXA scans: the T score is based on bone mass of young reference population

The T-score obtained from a DEXA scan is determined by comparing a patient's bone mineral density to the

bone mass of young adults of the same sex

. This reference group represents the peak bone mass, which serves as a benchmark for assessing bone loss. A T-score of -2.5 or below signifies osteoporosis, representing a significant reduction in bone density when compared to this optimal value. This standardised metric is crucial for diagnosing osteoporosis and gauging its severity relative to the ideal bone density levels attained during early adulthood.

The

average bone mass of a population of the same age and sex

is not used as the reference standard for T-scores in DEXA scans; rather, it pertains to Z-scores. The Z-score compares an individual's bone density with that of others who are similar in age, sex, and body size. Although useful for evaluating bone density in younger individuals or when exploring secondary causes of bone loss, the Z-score is not suitable in this context. The T-score specifically contrasts a patient’s bone mass with that of healthy young adults for the purpose of diagnosing osteoporosis and considering therapeutic interventions. Utilising the Z-score would fail to illuminate reductions in bone mass relative to peak levels, which is vital for accurate diagnosis.

The

average bone mass of a population with similar medical conditions

does not form the basis for calculating the T-score in DEXA scans. Instead, the T-score juxtaposes an individual's bone mass with that of healthy young adults irrespective of any health conditions they may have. Utilising comparisons with populations sharing similar medical conditions would not accurately reflect changes in bone density due to normal ageing or osteoporotic processes.

Furthermore, the

bone mass of elderly individuals

is not utilised when interpreting T-scores from DEXA scans because these scores are intended to compare an individual’s bone density with that of healthy young adults rather than older people. Such methodology is essential for detecting significant reductions in bone mass indicative of osteoporosis since age-related bone loss is anticipated and would seem less pronounced if contrasted with an elderly reference group. Therefore, employing older individuals as a benchmark could obscure decreases in bone density and complicate osteoporosis diagnosis.

Lastly, referencing the

bone mass of patients with a known history of osteoporosis

is unsuitable for determining T-scores since these scores rely on comparisons with healthy young adults' baseline values. The objective behind using T-scores is to discern deviations from normalcy in bone density to detect either osteoporosis or osteopenia. Using individuals already diagnosed with osteoporosis as a comparative measure would conceal true levels of bone loss relative to a healthy norm and impair the accurate assessment of condition severity.

question:
A 17-year-old male presents to General Practice with recurrent cramping in his arms during a rowing training session. On closer questioning, he has noticed a reduction in his exercise tolerance recently. He reports getting a 'second wind' phenomenon after minutes of rest.

On examination, he is well with no apparent deficit.

Bloods reveal:


Hb	142 g/l
Platelets	204 * 109/l
WBC	6.7 * 109/l
Na+	139 mmol/l
K+	4.2 mmol/l
Urea	8.9 mmol/l
Creatinine	148 µmol/l
Adjusted calcium	2.23 mmol/L
Creatine kinase	1037 IU/L
Autoimmune profile	pending

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

A 48-year-old woman presents with loss of sensation and weakness in her right hand. On examination, you ask the patient to pinch a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger against resistance. Her thumb interphalangeal joint flexes in response. You also note the loss of sensation to the medial 1.5 digits. There is no loss of sensation in the forearm.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cubital tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the ulnar nerve and can present with tingling/numbness of the 4th and 5th finger

This is a classical description of

cubital tunnel syndrome

. The ulnar nerve supplies sensory innervation to the palmar and dorsal aspects of 1.5 fingers medially. It has a motor component which can result in wasting and paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles (except lateral two lumbricals) and the hypothenar muscles. Froment's test as described in this case can be used to test the function of the adductor pollicis muscle which is often weak in ulnar neuropathy.

The

axillary nerve

has both a motor and a sensory distribution of innervation. It has motor fibres that innervate the deltoid muscle, acting as an abductor, flexor and extensor at the shoulder joint, as well as the teres minor muscle, allowing lateral rotation of the glenohumeral joint.  Its sensory function is from the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, which sweeps around the posterior border of the deltoid and supplies the skin over the lower two-thirds of the posterior part of this muscle, as well as that covering the long head of the triceps brachii.

Median nerve dysfunction results in

carpal tunnel syndrome

characterised by sensory loss over the lateral 3.5 digits, and loss of motor function to the flexor muscles of the forearm and hand as well as those muscles responsible for flexion, abduction, opposition, and extension of the thumb.

C8/T1 radiculopathy

can mimic ulnar nerve neuropathy.  In this case, the preserved sensation of the forearm favours a diagnosis of cubital tunnel syndrome. The ulnar nerve does not provide sensation to the medial forearm, which is innervated by the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve. C8 and T1 supply the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve via the medial cord of the brachial plexus, arising between the neck and proximal upper extremity.

The

radial nerve

innervates the muscles located in the posterior arm and posterior forearm. Dysfunction, therefore, results in loss of elbow and wrist extension. It also supplies sensation to the postero-lateral aspect of the hand.

question: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus after presenting with lethargy, arthralgia and a facial rash. Her rheumatologists starts her on hydroxychloroquine. Which one of the following is it most important to monitor?
explanation:
Hydroxychloroquine - may result in a severe and permanent retinopathy

The correct answer is

Visual acuity

. Hydroxychloroquine, an antimalarial drug, is commonly used in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The most significant and potentially serious side effect of hydroxychloroquine is retinopathy, which can lead to permanent vision loss. Therefore, it is crucial to monitor the patient's visual acuity regularly. According to the Royal College of Ophthalmologists in the UK, baseline eye screening should be performed within a year of starting treatment and then annually after five years of usage.

Blood pressure

monitoring may be important for patients with SLE as they may have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease due to chronic inflammation and corticosteroid use. However, it is not specifically related to hydroxychloroquine therapy.

Monitoring

Blood sugar

levels would be more relevant if the patient was started on corticosteroids or if they had a pre-existing condition like diabetes mellitus. Hydroxychloroquine does not typically cause hyperglycaemia.

QT interval on ECG

monitoring might be necessary when prescribing medications known to prolong the QT interval and increase the risk of torsades de pointes and other arrhythmias. Although hydroxychloroquine can theoretically prolong QT interval, this side effect is extremely rare in clinical practice so routine ECG monitoring isn't necessary unless there are other contributing factors.

Lastly,

Peak expiratory flow rate

would be monitored in conditions affecting lung function such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). There's no specific indication for its regular assessment in patients taking hydroxychloroquine unless they have a concurrent respiratory illness.

question:
A 43-year-old Chinese man is reviewed after describing painful paraesthesia affecting the palmar aspect of his right hand. He also reports occasional blood when passing urine. His past medical history is significant for chronic hepatitis B infection, for which he takes lamivudine.

On examination, he reports numbness and tenderness in the distribution of the ulnar nerve on the right hand side. He also has a patch of anaesthesia over the dorsum of his left foot.

His blood test results are shown below:


Hb	132 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	398 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	9.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	136 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.8 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	13.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	168 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	35 mg/L	(< 5)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa can cause a mononeuritis multiplex syndrome

This patient has a number of features of vasculitis, including haematuria with renal impairment, and a mildly raised CRP. The specific diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), a medium vessel vasculitis, is clinched by the presence of mononeuritis multiplex i.e. peripheral neuropathy affecting two or more non-contiguous nerve trunks, as well as hepatitis B infection, which is significantly associated with PAN.

Takayasu's arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis which comes with an increased risk of hypertension, aneurysms and hypertension. A textbook examination finding would be absent peripheral pulses.

Microscopic polyangiitis is a small vessel vasculitis that may also present with renal impairment and mildly raised inflammatory markers. However, the presence of mononeuritis multiplex and past medical history of hepatitis B, neither of which are associated with microscopic polyangiitis, make PAN more likely.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis classically involves renal impairment, as well as other disease features such as nasal congestion and epistaxis, rather than peripheral neuropathy.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-positive vasculitis which classically manifests with renal impairment and respiratory symptoms. For exam purposes, these patients often present with presumed asthma, which is difficult to control, with sensitivity to the prescription of leukotriene receptor antagonists. Blood eosinophilia is also observed.

question:
A 64-year-old man presents with acute-onset pain in the right knee. He describes it as incredibly intense; he has not had any previous episodes.

After examination of the knee, joint fluid is aspirated and sent to the lab. The rheumatology team are suspecting a diagnosis of pseudogout.

Which of the following features would aid in distinguishing this from gout?
options: Warmth at the site of pain
explanation:
Chondrocalcinosis helps to distinguish pseudogout from gout

The correct answer is chondrocalcinosis. This can be seen as linear calcifications of the meniscus and articular cartilage on an x-ray of the knee. This is seen in pseudogout, but not particularly associated with gout, and so it can be used to distinguish between the two.

Age is not a particularly distinguishing factor between gout and pseudogout. This patient is 64 years old; this does not sway the diagnosis one way or the other.

Simply the presence of crystals is not a distinguishing factor - they are present in both conditions. The type of crystals, however, differs between the two. Pseudogout crystals are weakly-positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped. Gout crystals are negatively birefringent.

Both conditions usually respond well to colchicine with regards to acute pain management, and so this is not a distinguishing factor.

There may be increased warmth of the affected joint in both conditions and so this is not a useful factor to distinguish between the two.

question: You review a 48-year-old woman who is taking methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. Concurrent prescription of which other medication should be avoided?
explanation:
The concurrent use of methotrexate and trimethoprim containing antibiotics may cause bone marrow suppression and severe or fatal pancytopaenia

The correct answer is

Trimethoprim

. Trimethoprim must be avoided in patients taking methotrexate due to a potentially dangerous drug interaction. Both medications inhibit dihydrofolate reductase, which converts dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, essential for DNA synthesis. When used together, there is a synergistic antifolate effect that can lead to severe bone marrow suppression, resulting in pancytopenia. This interaction can be life-threatening and is specifically contraindicated in prescribing guidelines.

Erythromycin

is a macrolide antibiotic that can be safely prescribed alongside methotrexate. While erythromycin can interact with various medications through its inhibition of CYP3A4, it does not significantly affect methotrexate metabolism or increase its toxicity.

Sumatriptan

, a 5-HT1 receptor agonist used for migraine treatment, has no significant interaction with methotrexate. These medications work through different mechanisms and can be safely co-prescribed if clinically indicated.

Lansoprazole

, a proton pump inhibitor, is actually often prescribed alongside methotrexate to reduce gastrointestinal side effects. While there are theoretical concerns about PPIs affecting methotrexate levels, this is not clinically significant at standard doses used in rheumatoid arthritis.

Sodium valproate

, an anticonvulsant and mood stabiliser, can be prescribed alongside methotrexate. While both medications require liver function monitoring, there is no direct interaction between these drugs that would preclude their concurrent use.

question: Which one of the following features is least typical of polymyalgia rheumatica?
options: Morning stiffness in proximal limb muscles

question: A 41-year-old man presents with persistent fatigue for the past 8 months. Which one of the following features is least consistent with a diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome?
options: Having a busy day improves the symptoms
correctText: Having a busy day improves the symptoms

question: A 31-year-old woman who had rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 5 years ago asks for advice as she is considering starting a family. She currently has quiescent rheumatoid arthritis which is well controlled on methotrexate. Which one of the following drugs is it safest to use if she is planning on becoming pregnant?

A 29-year-old woman presents with several months of an intermittently painful left hand, especially when outside in cold weather. She describes a spasming pain, associated with numbness and a colour change in the hand.

On examination, she is currently well and there are no signs or symptoms. Both hands appear normal. A non-specific, eczema-like rash is noted in the flexure creases.

Blood tests are taken and the patient is referred for more specialist testing.

What would point towards primary disease rather than secondary?
options: Positive findings on nailfold capillary microscopy
explanation:
Raynaud's disease (i.e. primary) presents in young women with bilateral symptoms

The history is highly suggestive of Raynaud's - spasming of the vessels of the hand, leading to colour changes, particularly in cold weather. Of the features listed above, the only one which points towards primary Raynaud's, rather than secondary, is the

age of onset under 40 years

. Primary Raynaud's is typically seen in young patients, under 30, as with this woman. Onset over 40 points more towards secondary Raynaud's (for instance, as part of a connective tissue disorder).

The scenario mentions specialist testing - this may involve

nail fold capillary microscopy

. Positive findings would indicate underlying pathology suggestive of secondary Raynaud's, rather than primary, and so this option is incorrect.

The

presence of autoantibodies

is also incorrect - these would indicate the possibility of a systemic disorder, such as systemic sclerosis, causing secondary Raynaud's.

The

rash

mentioned in the question is very non-specific and may just be eczema. The presence of a rash may be more indicative of secondary Raynaud's, as many systemic conditions that cause Raynaud's are also associated with rashes.

Unilateral symptoms

are again more indicative of secondary Raynaud's. The classic presentation of primary Raynaud's is that of bilateral symptoms.

question: Which one of the following drugs has been associated with an increased risk of atypical stress fractures of the proximal femoral shaft?
explanation:
Bisphosphonates are associated with an increased risk of atypical stress fractures

The correct answer is

Alendronate

. Alendronate is a bisphosphonate drug used in the treatment of osteoporosis and Paget's disease. It works by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, leading to an overall increase in total bone mass. However, long-term use of alendronate has been associated with atypical femoral fractures. These are stress or insufficiency fractures that occur in the subtrochanteric region or the shaft of the femur and are often bilateral. The mechanism behind this association is not fully understood but it is believed that suppression of bone turnover might lead to accumulation of microdamage within the bone, reducing its overall strength.

Spironolactone

, on the other hand, is a potassium-sparing diuretic used primarily to treat heart failure, liver cirrhosis, primary hyperaldosteronism and Conn's syndrome. Although it can cause gynaecomastia due to its anti-androgen effects, spironolactone has not been associated with an increased risk for atypical stress fractures.

Quetiapine

is an atypical antipsychotic medication used in the management of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. Its side effect profile includes weight gain, sedation and orthostatic hypotension but it does not increase the risk for atypical stress fractures.

Venlafaxine

, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), is used primarily for depression and anxiety disorders. While venlafaxine may cause side effects such as nausea, dizziness and hypertension among others, there have been no reports linking it with an increased risk for atypical stress fractures.

Finally,

Clopidogrel

is an antiplatelet agent used to prevent blood clots after a recent heart attack or stroke, and in people with certain disorders of the heart or blood vessels. Its most common side effects include bleeding and bruising but it does not predispose patients to atypical stress fractures.

question:
A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with reduced mobility. He describes finding it difficult to walk due to weakness in his left foot. There is no past medical history of note and he is normally fit and well and is a regular sports player.

On examination, there is reduced sensation in the lateral aspect of the left foot and posterior aspect of the left leg. He has normal power on dorsiflexion but reduced power on plantarflexion of his left foot. Ankle reflexes are lost.

Damage to what anatomical structure is likely to cause the patient's presentation?
explanation:
S1 lesion features = Sensory loss of posterolateral aspect of leg and lateral aspect of foot,  weakness in plantar flexion of foot, reduced ankle reflex, positive sciatic nerve stretch test

S1 nerve root

is correct. This patient has features of S1 nerve root impingement. The S1 nerve supplies sensation to the posterolateral aspect of the leg and lateral aspect of the foot. A lesion in the nerve also gives rise to a loss or weakness in the ankle reflex and weakness in plantarflexion.

Achilles tendon

is incorrect. An Achilles tendon rupture presents as a painful 'pop' sensation at the back of the heel. A positive Simmonds-Thompson test is seen where squeezing the calf muscle fails to cause plantarflexion of the foot. It would not account for the sensory loss seen in this patient.

Common fibular nerve

is incorrect. Injury to the common fibular nerve commonly occurs following injury to the neck of the fibular. It causes 'foot drop' and loss of dorsiflexion of the foot. This is not what is seen in this patient.

L4-L5 nerve root

is incorrect. The L4-L5 nerve roots supply sensation to the anterior knee and dorsum of the foot, respectively. Lesions or compression of these nerve roots causes weakness in the quadriceps and dorsiflexion of the foot and big toe.

Sural nerve

is incorrect. The sural nerve is a sensory nerve that supplies the lower posterolateral leg and lateral foot. Whilst the pattern of sensory loss is similar in this patient, the sural nerve carries no motor fibres and would not account for the weakness in plantarflexion, making an S1 nerve root injury more likely.

question: An 80-year-old woman is started on oral alendronate following a fractured neck of femur. How would you explain how to take the tablet?
options: Take it on a full stomach to minimise gastric irritation and avoid lying down for 30 minutes afterwards
Dissolve tablet in water and take just before breakfast + sit-upright for 30 minutes following
Take during main evening meal + sit-upright for 2 hours following
Take at least 30 minutes before breakfast with plenty of water + sit-upright for 30 minutes following
Take at least 30 minutes after a main meal + sit-upright for 30 minutes following
correctText: Take at least 30 minutes before breakfast with plenty of water + sit-upright for 30 minutes following
explanation:
Bisphosphonates can cause a variety of oesophageal problems

The correct answer is:

Take at least 30 minutes before breakfast with plenty of water + sit-upright for 30 minutes following

. Alendronate is a bisphosphonate used in the treatment of osteoporosis. It has poor oral bioavailability, which can be further reduced by food or drink (other than plain water). The absorption of alendronate is best when taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before the first food or drink of the day. Furthermore, due to its potential for causing oesophageal irritation and ulceration, it is recommended that patients remain upright (sitting or standing) for at least 30 minutes after ingestion to facilitate passage through the oesophagus.

Take it on a full stomach to minimise gastric irritation and avoid lying down for 30 minutes afterwards

: This statement is incorrect because taking alendronate with food significantly decreases its absorption. While avoiding lying down for 30 minutes afterwards is correct, it should be taken on an empty stomach.

Dissolve tablet in water and take just before breakfast + sit-upright for 30 minutes following

: This statement is incorrect as alendronate tablets should not be dissolved in water before consumption. They must be swallowed whole with plenty of water to avoid oesophageal irritation.

Take during main evening meal + sit-upright for 2 hours following

: This statement is incorrect because taking alendronate during meals reduces its absorption. Although remaining upright for two hours would not cause harm, UK guidelines recommend remaining upright for only 30 minutes post-ingestion.

Take at least 30 minutes after a main meal + sit-upright for 30 minutes following

: This statement is incorrect as taking alendronate after meals will reduce its absorption. It should be taken at least half an hour before the first food or drink of the day.

question: A 31-year-old woman presents as her fingers intermittently turn white and become painful. She describes the fingers first turning white, then blue and finally red. This is generally worse in the winter months but it is present all year round. Wearing gloves does not help. Clinical examination of her hands, other joints and skin is unremarkable. Which one of the following treatments may be beneficial?
explanation:
Nifedipine is a pharmacological option for Raynaud's phenomenon

Nifedipine

is the correct treatment option for this patient who is presenting with classic symptoms of Raynaud's phenomenon. The triphasic colour change (white, blue, then red) represents vasospasm of digital arteries, followed by cyanosis due to deoxygenated blood, and finally hyperaemia during reperfusion. Calcium channel blockers like nifedipine are first-line pharmacological therapy for Raynaud's phenomenon as they promote vasodilation of peripheral blood vessels, reducing the frequency and severity of vasospastic attacks. Nifedipine has been shown in multiple randomised controlled trials to decrease both the frequency and severity of attacks by approximately 30%. This patient's presentation is typical of primary Raynaud's disease, given her young age, female gender, and absence of signs suggesting an underlying connective tissue disorder (normal joint and skin examination). The lack of response to simple measures like wearing gloves indicates that pharmacological treatment is appropriate.

Propranolol

is contraindicated in Raynaud's phenomenon and would likely worsen this patient's symptoms. Beta-blockers cause peripheral vasoconstriction through unopposed alpha-adrenergic activity, which can exacerbate vasospastic attacks. In fact, beta-blockers are known to precipitate or worsen Raynaud's phenomenon and should be avoided in these patients. If a patient with hypertension and Raynaud's phenomenon requires antihypertensive therapy, calcium channel blockers would be preferred over beta-blockers for this reason.

Amitriptyline

is not indicated for Raynaud's phenomenon. While amitriptyline is used for various pain conditions including neuropathic pain, it does not address the underlying vasospasm that characterises Raynaud's phenomenon. Amitriptyline has no significant vasodilatory effects that would benefit the peripheral circulation in this condition. Additionally, some tricyclic antidepressants can actually cause vasoconstriction as a side effect, which could potentially worsen symptoms in some patients with Raynaud's phenomenon.

Aspirin

is not a first-line treatment for primary Raynaud's phenomenon. While aspirin has antiplatelet effects that may be beneficial in conditions with thrombotic risk, the pathophysiology of Raynaud's primarily involves vasospasm rather than thrombosis. In severe secondary Raynaud's phenomenon associated with conditions like scleroderma, where there may be a risk of digital ulceration, antiplatelet therapy might be considered as part of a comprehensive management plan, but it would not be appropriate as primary therapy for this patient with likely primary Raynaud's disease.

Losartan

, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), is not a first-line treatment for Raynaud's phenomenon. While some studies have suggested that losartan may have modest benefits in reducing the frequency and severity of attacks in some patients with primary and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, the evidence is not as robust as for calcium channel blockers. The mechanism may involve improved endothelial function and reduced oxidative stress rather than direct vasodilation. Losartan might be considered as an alternative in patients who cannot tolerate calcium channel blockers, but it would not be the first choice for this patient with classic Raynaud's symptoms.

question: A 22-year-old man attends the cardiology clinic for review of a recently diagnosed heart murmur. He is tall with long fingers and has mild scoliosis. On examination, he has high-arched palate and pes planus. Ophthalmological assessment reveals impaired vision in one eye, and slit-lamp examination confirms lens dislocation upwards and outwards. Which underlying diagnosis most likely explains this pattern of features?
explanation:
Marfan's syndrome - upwards lens dislocation

Marfan's syndrome

is the correct answer because it is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene, resulting in abnormal fibrillin-1. Classic features include tall stature, arachnodactyly, high-arched palate, scoliosis, pectus abnormalities, pes planus, and cardiovascular manifestations such as aortic root dilation or mitral valve prolapse. Ocular involvement commonly includes ectopia lentis—specifically superotemporal (upwards/outwards) lens dislocation—which distinguishes Marfan’s from other syndromes with similar systemic features. Recognising this specific direction of lens displacement is key to differentiating Marfan’s from close differentials.

Homocystinuria

shares many phenotypic similarities with Marfan’s (tall stature, lens dislocation), but the direction of lens displacement in homocystinuria is typically inferonasal (downwards/inwards). It also often presents earlier with intellectual disability and thromboembolic events; neither are mentioned here.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

can present with joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility and sometimes marfanoid habitus; however, it does not characteristically cause ectopia lentis or upward lens dislocation. Cardiovascular complications differ as well.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B

may be associated with a marfanoid body habitus but lacks the ophthalmological findings described here. It more commonly presents with mucosal neuromas and medullary thyroid carcinoma rather than connective tissue or ocular features.

Stickler syndrome

can have ocular involvement (including myopia and retinal detachment) along with joint hypermobility and craniofacial abnormalities such as cleft palate; however, it does not typically present with upward lens dislocation or the classical combination of skeletal features seen here.

question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of dry mouth, difficulty swallowing dry foods, and a persistent need to drink water throughout the day. She also reports dry eyes, occasional joint pain, and fatigue.

On examination, her oral mucosa appears dry, and she has evidence of tooth decay. Schirmer’s test is positive, and blood tests reveal positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies.

Given the most likely diagnosis what medication should be commenced to address her dry mouth?
explanation:
Sjogren's syndrome: pilocarpine may be helpful to stimulate saliva production

The diagnosis, in this case, is most likely Sjögren’s syndrome due to the combination of dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, dry eyes, and fatigue, alongside positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, which are hallmark diagnostic features of this autoimmune condition. Sjögren’s primarily affects exocrine glands, leading to reduced saliva and tear production.

Pilocarpine

is correct because it is a muscarinic receptor agonist that stimulates salivary gland function, increasing saliva production to alleviate the dry mouth symptoms described. It is particularly effective in cases where residual salivary gland function remains, enhancing secretion rather than reversing gland damage. By addressing xerostomia, pilocarpine improves swallowing, reduces oral discomfort, and minimises the risk of dental complications, directly targeting the patient’s main concern and improving their quality of life.

Duloxetine

is incorrect because it is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor primarily used for treating depression, anxiety, and chronic pain. While it can manage pain, it does not stimulate saliva production and is not effective for dry mouth in Sjögren's syndrome. Furthermore, it does not have any established role in stimulating salivation, making it an unsuitable choice for this condition.

Hyoscine hydrobromide

is incorrect because it is an antimuscarinic drug used for motion sickness and nausea by blocking acetylcholine receptors. However, it can cause dry mouth as a side effect by inhibiting salivation, which makes it unsuitable for managing dry mouth in Sjögren's syndrome. Using this drug could worsen the symptoms of dry mouth rather than alleviate them.

Neostigmine

is incorrect because it is a cholinesterase inhibitor that increases acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions, used primarily to treat myasthenia gravis. Although it could increase salivation, it is not typically used for managing dry mouth in Sjögren’s syndrome because its primary use is for muscle strength improvement, not for stimulating salivation. It also has a more targeted action at the neuromuscular junction rather than salivary glands.

Nortriptyline

is incorrect because it is a tricyclic antidepressant with anticholinergic properties. It inhibits the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine but can cause dry mouth as a side effect, making it unsuitable for patients with Sjögren’s syndrome who need salivation stimulation. Its anticholinergic effects would worsen dry mouth rather than help alleviate it.

question:
A 42-year-old man is admitted to hospital with a 6-week history of cough, weight loss and occasional haemoptysis. A chest X-ray demonstrates fibronodular opacities and sputum acid-fast bacilli smear is positive. A diagnosis of tuberculosis is made and he is started on a combination of medications.

Subsequently, he develops a malar rash, arthralgia and myalgia. Blood tests are taken:


Antinuclear antibodies	Positive
Anti-dsDNA antibodies	Negative
Anti-histone antibodies	Positive

Given the new findings, which drug is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Isoniazid can cause drug-induced lupus

The correct answer is isoniazid. The findings describe drug-induced lupus which presents with some, but not all, of the typical features of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). It usually resolves once the offending drug is stopped. Anti-histone antibodies are typically positive when lupus is drug-induced, and less commonly so in SLE. Conversely, anti-dsDNA antibodies are seen in more than half of SLE cases, but very rarely in drug-induced lupus. The most common drug causes include procainamide and hydralazine. However, from the list of tuberculosis antibiotics (and pyridoxine), the most likely cause is isoniazid. This antibiotic is known to cause drug-induced lupus. Other side effects include peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis.

Ethambutol is another antibiotic given as part of tuberculosis management. It is not known to cause drug-induced lupus. One of its key side effects includes optic neuritis and so visual acuity should be checked before and during treatment.

Pyrazinamide is another tuberculosis antibiotic. It is not known to cause drug-induced lupus, but can cause gout due to increasing uric acid levels and may cause hepatitis.

Pyridoxine is vitamin B6. This should be given to all patients taking isoniazid, as the latter can disrupt vitamin B6 levels which may lead to peripheral neuropathy. It is not known to cause drug-induced lupus.

Rifampicin, another antibiotic used for tuberculosis, has very rarely been linked to drug-induced lupus - although this may be confounded by concurrent administration of isoniazid, which remains the most likely cause here. Side effects include hepatitis, orange secretions and flu-like symptoms.

question:
A 36-year-old patient presents with a facial rash and joint pains. She has a history of recurrent miscarriages and had a deep vein thrombosis at the age of 19.

On examination, there is a butterfly-shaped rash on her cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds. Tenderness and swelling affect the small joints of her hands bilaterally. Her temperature is 37.8ºC.

Given the likely diagnosis, what result best supports the presence of active disease?
explanation:
SLE: complement levels (C3, C4) are usually low during active disease - may be used to monitor flares

Low complement levels

is correct. This patient presents with a malar rash (butterfly rash that spares the nasolabial folds) and synovitis. Along with the history of recurrent miscarriage and previous venous thromboembolism, this suggests a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with secondary anti-phospholipid syndrome. Complement levels (C3 and C4) are typically low in active disease - that is, related to disease activity.

Low anti-dsDNA antibodies

is incorrect. High anti-dsDNA antibody levels typically suggest active disease in SLE.

Polycythaemia

is incorrect. Patients with SLE may be anaemic for a variety of causes such as anaemia of chronic disease, haemolytic anaemia or aplastic anaemia. Some of those states may be related to active disease. However, polycythaemia - raised haemoglobin - is not typically a feature of active SLE.

Positive ANA

is incorrect. The ANA must be positive to obtain a diagnosis of SLE. However, it is not related to whether the disease is currently active.

Positive lupus anticoagulant

is incorrect. This may be positive in antiphospholipid syndrome and indeed this patient may have this diagnosis. However, it has no relation to whether the disease is active or not.

question:
A 53-year-old woman with a background of seropositive non-erosive rheumatoid arthritis presents to the rheumatology outpatient clinic with pain and swelling in her hands, feet and shoulders. She is currently taking sulfasalazine as disease-modifying therapy. She has not trialled any other disease-modifying agents for rheumatoid arthritis. She is post-menopausal.

On examination, she has 7 tender and 5 swollen joints. The CRP is 35mg/L. Her patient global health score is 70/100. She has a DAS28-CRP of 5.34, indicating high disease activity.

Her rheumatologist decides to add an additional disease-modifying drug anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD).

What is the mechanism of action of the next logical medication choice?
explanation:
Methotrexate works by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase

Anti-TNF monoclonal antibody is not the right answer. A different class of medications used to treated rheumatoid arthritis known as 'anti-TNF' biologic medications work by this mechanism of action. This class of medication is typically reserved for those patients who have trialled at least two conventional DMARDs (i.e. sulfasalazine, methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine or leflunomide) and have persistently high disease activity (DAS28-CRP or DAS28-ESR > 5.1). They include etanercept, adalimumab, certolizumab, golimumab and infliximab. They are the first line biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug in the absence of contraindications.

Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase is the correct answer. This is the mechanism of action of methotrexate, which is considered to be an 'anchor' drug in rheumatoid arthritis. Before progressing to trying some of the newer biologic medications, patients with rheumatoid arthritis must try at least two conventional disease-modifying therapies (i.e. sulfasalazine, methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine or leflunomide). Hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide are not listed as answers to this question. One of the two medications trialled should be methotrexate unless contraindicated.

Inhibition of janus kinase is incorrect. This is the mechanism of action used by medications such as baricitinib to treat rheumatoid arthritis. Specifically, baricitinib blocks the subtypes JAK1 and JAK2 of janus kinase. Again, patients must typically trial at least two conventional DMARDs before being commenced on this type of medication.

Inhibition of IL-6 is the wrong answer. This is the mechanism by which tocilizumab exerts its anti-rheumatic effects. It is another biologic disease-modifying drug that can only be trialled after conventional DMARD medications.

Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody is also the wrong answer. This is the mechanism of action of rituximab. It is another biologic medication used for patients with severe rheumatoid arthritis. It is typically trialled only after the use of conventional DMARDs and an anti-TNF biologic have failed.

question:
A 48-year-old man presents to the emergency department with reports of abdominal pain, fever, joint swelling and sharp chest pain. This constellation of symptoms has affected him on three previous occasions, resolving after 1-3 days. He is originally from Turkey.

Observations:


Heart rate 82 beats per minute
Blood pressure 120/77 mmHg
Temperature 38.4ºC

On examination, there the abdomen is mildly tender throughout. There is synovitis affecting the left ankle and right knee. Leaning forward eases his chest pain.

The patient is treated with colchicine and rapidly improves.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal recessive, hereditary inflammatory disorder characterised by reoccurring episodes of abdominal pain, fever, arthralgia, and chest pain

Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is the correct answer. Tel-Hashomer diagnostic criteria are used to diagnose FMF. This patient meets these classification criteria on the basis of recurrent episodes of serositis (peritonitis, synovitis, pericarditis) in association with fever and prompt response to colchicine. FMF is more common in people of Turkish descent.

Reactive arthritis is incorrect. Typically, this is characterized by arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis. Peritonitis and pericarditis are not typical and this is, therefore, less likely.

Behcet's syndrome is incorrect. This disorder is common in those of Turkish descent. However, it is characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulceration, which is absent in this case.

Dressler's syndrome is incorrect. This is a cause of post myocardial infarction pericarditis. It would explain the chest pain in this presentation but not anything else and is therefore unlikely.

Gout is incorrect. This can cause synovitis that would respond to colchicine. However, pericarditis and peritonitis are not features and it is therefore not the likely diagnosis.

question:
A 28-year-old man presents to rheumatology clinic with a 2-year history of progressive lower back pain and stiffness, worse in the morning and improving with activity. He also reports occasional heel pain. On examination, there is reduced lumbar spine mobility. HLA-B27 is positive. X-ray of the spine shows vertical ossification along the anterolateral aspects of adjacent vertebrae.

What is the most likely radiological finding described?
explanation:
Syndesmophytes (ossification of outer fibres of annulus fibrosus) are a feature of ankylosing spondylitis

Syndesmophytes

are the most likely radiological finding described in this case. Syndesmophytes are vertical ossifications that occur along the anterolateral aspects of adjacent vertebrae due to ossification of the outer fibres of the annulus fibrosus. They are a characteristic feature of ankylosing spondylitis (AS), which is strongly suggested by this patient's clinical presentation. The young male patient with progressive inflammatory back pain (worse in the morning, improving with activity), reduced spinal mobility, and positive HLA-B27 fits the typical profile for AS. Syndesmophytes are formed when inflammation at the discovertebral junction leads to ossification that grows vertically, parallel to the outer fibres of the annulus fibrosus, eventually bridging adjacent vertebrae. This is distinct from the horizontal osteophytes seen in degenerative disc disease.

Bamboo spine

refers to the advanced radiographic appearance in ankylosing spondylitis where complete fusion of the vertebral bodies occurs due to extensive syndesmophyte formation, giving the spine a bamboo-like appearance on lateral radiographs. This represents a late finding in the disease process and would be described as complete fusion of vertebrae rather than vertical ossifications along the anterolateral aspects. The patient's relatively short 2-year history suggests earlier radiographic changes rather than this advanced finding.

Sacroiliitis

refers to inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, which is indeed a hallmark feature of ankylosing spondylitis and typically one of the earliest radiographic findings. However, the description in the question specifically refers to findings in the spine (vertical ossification along anterolateral aspects of adjacent vertebrae), not the sacroiliac joints, making this answer incorrect for the described radiological finding.

Squaring of vertebral bodies

is another radiographic feature of ankylosing spondylitis where erosion and subsequent sclerosis of the anterior corners of vertebral bodies creates a squared appearance. While this may be present in this patient, the description of vertical ossification along the anterolateral aspects of adjacent vertebrae more specifically describes syndesmophytes rather than vertebral squaring.

Osteophytes

are bony outgrowths that typically project horizontally from the vertebral body margins and are characteristic of degenerative disc disease rather than inflammatory spondyloarthropathies like ankylosing spondylitis. Osteophytes form from the vertebral rim and extend horizontally or obliquely, whereas syndesmophytes grow vertically and parallel to the outer annulus fibrosus. The clinical picture and the description of vertical ossification are not consistent with osteophytes.

question: A 35-year-old woman who has severe Raynaud's disease is reviewed in clinic. Three months ago she was started on nifedipine. Unfortunately this has had a minimal effect on her symptoms and has resulted in ankle oedema. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Epoprostenol (amongst other prostaglandins) can be used in the treatment of Raynaud's phenomenon

The correct answer is

intravenous prostacyclin

. In severe Raynaud's disease that has failed to respond to first-line calcium channel blockers like nifedipine, intravenous prostacyclin (iloprost) is the recommended next step in management according to UK guidelines. Prostacyclin is a potent vasodilator that helps improve peripheral circulation and can provide significant symptomatic relief in severe cases.

Aspirin

has a limited role in Raynaud's disease. While it may be used in some cases, particularly if there is underlying vascular disease, it is not considered an effective treatment for severe symptoms that have failed calcium channel blocker therapy.

Sympathectomy
