Septic arthritis is a serious condition caused by an infection in a joint. Typically this is due to spread from an extra-articular infection, such as pneumonia or cellulitis. It is commonly associated with marked systemic upset, elevated inflammatory markers, and rapid progression (hours to days)

Slipped upper femoral epiphysis is a condition affecting children; largely, overweight children. It presents as a painful limp. Adults, in whom the femoral epiphysis is fused to the rest of the femur, cannot develop this condition. It is therefore not the correct answer in this case.

question:
An 8-year-old boy presents to the general practitioner with his father. His father reports that he has noticed the child's wrists have become swollen over the past few months. There is no history of any trauma and the boy has no other past medical history.

On examination the child is underweight and appears malnourished. He is alert and otherwise systemically well. Bony swellings are noted in both wrists.

Blood tests and an X-ray are ordered.


Bilirubin	7 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	312 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	31 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	16 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	36 g/L	(35 - 50)


X-ray both wrists	cupping and fraying of the metaphyseal region

What is the pathophysiological process causing this child's symptoms?
options: Excessive activity of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Î’ ligand (RANKL)
explanation:
Rickets can present as widening of the wrist joints due to an excess of non-mineralized osteoid at the growth plate

This boy has rickets as evidenced by his swollen wrists, raised ALP and disturbance of the metaphyseal region on X-ray. Rickets is caused by a deficiency in vitamin D or calcium, usually due to poor dietary intake. Calcium is required for the mineralisation of osteoid and formation of mature bone tissue. If this cannot occur, a build up of this non-mineralised osteoid bone results in rickets disease.

RANKL is an enzyme that is targeted by monoclonal antibodies in the treatment of osteoporosis. It ordinarily activates osteoclasts, promoting bone resorption. It is not the cause of rickets.

Excessive mineralised osteoid is incorrect here. The cause of rickets is inadequate calcium for mineralisation, hence the build up of non-mineralised osteoid.

Excessive osteoclast activity can cause diseases such as osteoporosis and Paget's disease however is not the cause of rickets.

Deficiency of osteoclast activity can result in osteopetrosis but not rickets.

question:
A 23-year-old male is under review by the GP following insidiously worsening lower back pain. The pain is worse in the morning and after periods of inactivity. Over the preceding 6 months, he also reports increasing fatigue. Symptoms improved dramatically after the GP commenced regular NSAIDs. A lumbar spine x-ray is performed which is suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis.

Which of the following is most likely to be seen on the patient's x-ray?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis - x-ray findings: subchondral erosions, sclerosis

The correct answer is subchondral erosions. These are typically seen in the corners of vertebral bodies and on the iliac side of the sacroiliac joint, preceded by subchondral sclerosis. Squaring of the lumbar vertebrae consequently occurs, leading to a characteristic bamboo spine appearance.

Juxta-articular osteoporosis is typically observed in rheumatoid arthritis, often affecting joints of the hand, not the lumbar spine.

Loss of vertebral height is incorrect; this would be observed in vertebral body compression fractures.

Osteopenia occurring in a 23-year-old would likely be caused by malnutrition or malabsorptive disorders. It is not directly caused by ankylosing spondylitis.

Vertebral body wedging has multiple etiologies, including fractures, scoliosis and spina-bifida. It is not seen in ankylosing spondylitis.

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents with a facial rash that appears to be worse in summer. She has also noticed intermittent swelling of the small joints of her hands and describes suffering from Raynaud's syndrome for 5 years.

Given the likely diagnosis which of these auto-antibodies is most likely to be positive?

A 53-year-old woman presents to her GP complaining of progressively worsening wrist pain that began about a week ago. The pain is concentrated on the radial side. She plays tennis five times a week and enjoys gardening in her leisure time. She does not remember any injury before the onset of the pain and has no other medical history.

On examination, she exhibits marked tenderness over the radial styloid process, and thumb abduction is painful, especially against resistance.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pain on the radial side of the wrist/tenderness over the radial styloid process ? De Quervain's tenosynovitis

De Quervain's tenosynovitis

is the correct answer. The patient presents with a gradual onset of pain on the radial aspect of the wrist, accompanied by increased tenderness over the radial styloid, without preceding trauma but with a history of repetitive wrist use through activities such as tennis and gardening. These clinical features are suggestive of de quervain's tenosynovitis, which is characterised by inflammation of the synovial sheath that encases the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus tendons. Chronic repetitive movements can lead to inflammation of these tendons, resulting in symptoms as described in this case. Finkelstein's test is indicative of this condition; it involves ulnar deviation and longitudinal traction of the thumb by an examiner, eliciting increased pain over the radial styloid process when positive.

Arthritis of carpometacarpal joint

is incorrect. While arthritis at this joint should be considered in patients presenting with similar symptoms, it typically has a more insidious onset and may involve other joints concurrently, which is not demonstrated in this patient.

Carpal tunnel syndrome

is incorrect. This condition involves compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. Although there can be weakness in thumb abduction similar to what has been noted in this patient, typical symptoms include disturbances affecting the distribution area of the thumb, index, and middle fingers rather than being isolated around just one digit. Repetitive wrist and finger movements are also risk factors for developing carpal tunnel syndrome.

Lateral epicondylitis

is incorrect. Commonly associated with new or strenuous activities like house painting or playing tennis, lateral epicondylitis causes pain localized at the elbow rather than at the wrist as observed in this case. Additionally, patients usually experience exacerbated pain upon wrist extension against resistance when their elbow is extended – distinct from pain during thumb abduction against resistance seen here.

Scaphoid fracture

is incorrect. This diagnosis should be carefully considered due to its potential for being overlooked and leading to avascular necrosis if untreated; however, it typically follows a traumatic event such as a fall onto an outstretched hand – absent in this patient’s history. Clinical signs would likely include swelling due to effusion and maximal tenderness overlying the anatomical snuffbox rather than overlying the radial styloid as described here.

question: A 43-year-old woman presents with pain in the right elbow. This has been present for the past month and she reports no obvious trigger. On examination she reports pain on wrist extension against resistance whilst the elbow is extended. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Which one of the following statements regarding ankylosing spondylitis is correct?
options: Schober's test assesses reduced chest expansion
HLA-B27 is positive in 50% of patients
Achilles tendonitis is a recognised association
It is equally common in men and women
The typical age of presentation is between 40-50 years
correctText: Achilles tendonitis is a recognised association
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis features - the 'A's

The correct answer is

Achilles tendonitis is a recognised association

. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic, inflammatory arthritis and autoimmune disease that primarily affects the axial skeleton. It can lead to various extra-articular manifestations, one of which includes Achilles tendonitis. This occurs due to enthesitis, inflammation of the areas where tendons or ligaments insert into the bone, which is a characteristic feature of AS.

Schober's test assesses reduced chest expansion

is incorrect. Schober's test is used in the assessment of lumbar spine mobility and not chest expansion. In AS, chest expansion may be reduced due to costovertebral joint involvement leading to the fusion of the ribs with the vertebrae; however, this is assessed by measuring the circumference of the chest at full inspiration and expiration.

The statement

HLA-B27 is positive in 50% of patients

is also incorrect. Although HLA-B27 antigen has been associated with AS, it's positivity rate in patients with AS is much higher than 50%. According to UK guidelines and research studies, about 90-95% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis are HLA-B27 positive.

It is equally common in men and women

, this statement isn't accurate either. Ankylosing spondylitis shows a male predominance. It's approximately two to three times more common in men than women.

Lastly,

The typical age of presentation is between 40-50 years

isn't true as well. The typical age of onset for ankylosing spondylitis tends to be much younger than this range suggests. Most commonly, individuals present in late adolescence or early adulthood (ages 20-30). The onset after age 40 years old would be considered atypical for ankylosing spondylitis.

question:
A 42-year-old woman presents with a long-standing history of proximal muscle weakness and discomfort as well as skin changes affecting multiple areas of her body.

On examination, she has a purplish, 'heliotrope' rash around the eyes along with periorbital swelling, Gottron's papules over the extensor surface of the fingers and extremely dry skin of the hands.

Blood tests show a raised creatinine kinase level and the diagnosis is confirmed via electromyography and muscle biopsy.

What antibody is most associated with this patient's conditions?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis is associated with the anti-Jo-1 antibody

This patient has presented with the hallmark features of the inflammatory disorder dermatomyositis, presenting with both proximal muscle and skin disruption. The diagnosis is typically confirmed with patients meeting five criteria; these two features plus raised serum muscle enzymes (e.g. creatinine kinase), white blood cells between the muscle cells on biopsy and finally erratic, repetitive and high-frequency signals on electromyography. Several antibodies are associated with the condition, the most common of which is antinuclear antibodies (ANA) but a significant percentage of patients with the condition are also found to have

anti-Jo-1

antibodies also.

Anti-Ro antibodies

, also known as anti-SSA, are associated with several autoimmune conditions, most commonly SLE, neonatal lupus and primary biliary cirrhosis. They can also be found to be positive in other autoimmune conditions such as dermatomyositis but far less frequently than other antibodies including anti-Jo-1.

Anti-topoisomerase (

anti-Scl-70

) antibodies are mainly seen in patients with diffuse systemic scleroderma although they are also found in the more limited form CREST syndrome (calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia). Anti-Scl-70 is typically found to be negative in dermatomyositis patients.

Anti-centromere

antibodies are associated with the limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis, also known as CREST syndrome, referring to the 5 main features of calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. They are not associated with dermatomyositis.

Anti-nRNP

antibodies are autoantibodies against specific ribonucleoprotein which play a role in RNA production and regulation. These antibodies can be raised in mixed connective tissue disease however they have relatively low sensitivity and specificity and therefore are not commonly tested for.

question:
A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue and shortness of breath. He has a history of pulmonary and renal sarcoidosis which is treated with an immunosuppressive agent.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	45 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	28 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	1.1 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	0.1 * 10 9/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	0.8 * 10 9/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.1 * 10 9/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	0.1 * 10 9/L	(0.0 - 0.4)
Ferritin	140 ng/mL	(20 - 230)
Vitamin B12	560 ng/L	(200 - 900)
Folate	5.4 nmol/L	(> 3.0)
Reticulocytes	0.1 %	(0.5 - 1.5)
TPMT	5 nmol/h/g Hb	(26 - 50)

What medication is likely implicated?
explanation:
Azathioprine - check thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency (TPMT) before treatment

Azathioprine

is correct. The patient's blood results indicate pancytopenia (low counts of red and white blood cells and platelets). This can be a side effect of several immunosuppressive agents, but the low TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase) level points towards azathioprine. Azathioprine is metabolised to mercaptopurine by TPMT. Individuals with low TPMT activity are at risk of azathioprine toxicity, which can present as bone marrow suppression leading to pancytopenia. Therefore, in this patient with low TPMT levels and pancytopenia, azathioprine is the likely culprit. However, in an ideal setting, the patient's TPMT status should have been determined prior to the commencement of azathioprine.

Cyclosporin

is incorrect. Metabolism of this agent is not dependent upon TPMT levels making this a less likely choice.

Infliximab

is incorrect. Metabolism of this agent is not dependent upon TPMT levels making this a less likely choice.

Methotrexate

is incorrect. Metabolism of this agent is not dependent upon TPMT levels making this a less likely choice.

Mycophenolate mofetil

is incorrect. Metabolism of this agent is not dependent upon TPMT levels making this a less likely choice.

question:
A 62-year-old woman presents to her GP with several months of pain and stiffness in both knees and the hands. She also describes some swelling of the left index finger. She is otherwise well, with no significant past medical history except for hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine, and a cough which is currently under investigation.

On examination, she has dactylitis of the left index finger, as well as generalised pain and poor mobility of the fingers. X-rays of the hands are taken:


Hand X-rays	Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint erosions bilaterally.

Which diagnosis would be most typical of the findings?
explanation:
Inflammatory arthritis involving DIP swelling and dactylitis points to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis

The diagnosis here is that of psoriatic arthritis. The correlation between this and cutaneous psoriasis is actually quite poor and arthritic symptoms often precede skin lesions. There is significant overlap with rheumatoid arthritis in terms of presentation, but the features of DIP joint disease and dactylitis point much more towards psoriatic arthritis rather than rheumatoid.

Gout is incorrect - this would be more acute and monoarticular or oligoarticular. It would not present with the other symptoms seen here.

Osteoarthritis is incorrect. This would more commonly present asymmetrically, of a larger joint, and not have features such as dactylitis present, nor the findings on X-ray.

Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Whilst some degree of overlap, as described above, DIP joint disease would be less likely, as well as dactylitis. A blood test should be undertaken to look for anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (anti-CCP) as these have a very high degree of specificity for rheumatoid arthritis, and are usually absent in psoriatic arthritis.

Sarcoid dactylitis is incorrect. Dactylitis is found in some patients with chronic sarcoid, but would not present with this patient's X-ray findings, and the patient would have other features of sarcoidosis. A cough is mentioned in the history as a red herring but this would not explain the other symptoms and X-ray findings in this scenario, and so psoriatic arthritis is still far more likely.

question:
A 47-year-old woman has returned to the clinic for the results of recent investigations.

She was initially referred with a persistent rash. It was noted to involve multiple areas of her body, but the worst areas were a v-shaped, scaly rash affecting the upper chest and with scales affecting her metacarpophalangeal joints.

The examination also demonstrated evidence of muscle weakness with the patient struggling to stand from a sitting position whilst her arms were crossed. She had mild effusions in her elbows and knees and during the consultation was noted to have a cough.

A rheumatoid screening profile was sent to confirm the diagnosis.

Given the likely diagnosis, which is the most specific antibody in this condition?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis antibodies: ANA most common, anti-Mi-2 most specific

Anti-RNP is very specific for mixed connective tissue disease but can also be seen in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Anti-Ro (also known as anti-SSA) has a high specificity for Sjogren's syndrome. It can also be found in primary biliary cirrhosis and SLE.

Anti-centromere is specific for limited systemic scleroderma and is sometimes seen in diffuse scleroderma.

c-ANCA is specific in granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Anti-Mi-2 is correct and is highly specific in dermatomyositis. The scenario describes a v-shaped chest rash with a phalangeal joint rash which are both commonly found in the condition. It is also common to suffer from proximal muscle weakness and sometimes shortness of breath and cough can be present.

question:
A 39-year-old man is referred to orthopaedics with a 24-hour history of knee pain. He undergoes aspiration and urgent gram stain shows no organisms or crystals but many white blood cells.

You are asked for a medical opinion. When you review the patient you note chemosis and watery discharge of both eyes and he reports dysuria for several days. He reports he is sexually active with one partner and they always use condoms. On further questioning, he reveals he had an episode of diarrhoea 3 weeks previously which resolved after 4 days.

What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Administer IM benzathine penicillin and refer to sexual health services
Start non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and refer to rheumatology
Take blood cultures and start IV flucloxacillin
correctText: Start non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and refer to rheumatology
explanation:
Reactive arthritis: develops after an infection where the organism cannot be recovered from the joint

The correct answer is

start non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and refer to rheumatology

. This patient has the classic triad of reactive arthritis (formerly known as Reiter's syndrome) - arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis. The recent episode of diarrhoea may have represented

Campylobacter

or

Salmonella

infection, which are common triggers for this condition.

Administer IM benzathine penicillin and refer to sexual health services

is incorrect. This would be a treatment option for syphilis, which can present with synovitis. However, it usually presents with migratory polyarthritis rather than the monoarthritis described here. It would also not explain urethritis or recent diarrhoeal illness.

Organise joint washout

is incorrect. This would be recommended in cases of septic arthritis in conjunction with appropriate IV antibiotics. However, the negative gram stain in the absence of recent antibiotic exposure makes septic arthritis unlikely here and invasive management would be inappropriate without good evidence of the diagnosis.

Start IV ceftriaxone

is incorrect. This would be the treatment of choice for gonococcal arthritis. This can present with monoarthritis and a negative gram stain, but more commonly is seen in the context of disseminated gonococcal infection - this presents with dermatitis, polyarthritis and tenosynovitis. His sexual history also does not imply a high risk of this. It would also be unlikely to explain the recent diarrhoeal illness.

Take blood cultures and start IV flucloxacillin

is incorrect. This would be appropriate for septic arthritis, with the most common organisms being

Staphylococcus aureus

and beta-haemolytic streptococci. However, it is unusual to have a negative gram stain in such cases in the absence of recent antibiotic therapy. This would also not explain the ocular or urethral symptoms or the recent diarrhoeal illness.

question:
A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a laceration on his forearm sustained while gardening. He reports a tendency to bruise easily and often notices unexplained bruising on various parts of his body. His medical history includes recurrent joint dislocations, and he notes a family history of similar symptoms in his father.

On examination, his skin demonstrates marked elasticity, and he exhibits hypermobility in several joints.

What genetic defect most accurately accounts for his clinical presentation?
explanation:
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is most commonly associated with a defect in type III collagen

A

type III collagen defect

causes vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which leads to weakened skin and blood vessels. This defect explains the patient's easy bruising and skin hyperelasticity, making the skin prone to lacerations even with minor trauma. Additionally, joint hypermobility due to weakened ligaments results in recurrent joint dislocations, directly correlating with the patient's symptoms.

Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (kEDS), caused by a

defect in lysyl hydroxylase

, leads to connective tissue fragility, scoliosis, and muscle weakness. While joint hypermobility and skin hyperelasticity can be present, the absence of scoliosis and muscle weakness in this patient makes kEDS less likely.

Another possible condition is Marfan syndrome, caused by a

mutation in the fibrillin-1

gene. This syndrome is associated with tall stature, joint hypermobility, and cardiovascular issues, particularly aortic dilation. However, it does not typically cause skin hyperelasticity or easy bruising, which are key features of this patient's presentation.

Type I collagen defects

are most commonly associated with Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI). OI primarily affects the bones, leading to brittle bones and frequent fractures, not the skin or joints. Although joint hypermobility can occur in OI, skin hyperelasticity and easy bruising are not characteristic, ruling out this diagnosis.

Type IV collagen defects

lead to Alport syndrome, which primarily causes progressive renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities. This syndrome does not involve skin hyperelasticity, easy bruising, or joint hypermobility, making it an unlikely cause of this patient's symptoms.

question:
A 44-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a 6-week history of joint pain and stiffness, affecting his fingers and wrists. His symptoms are worst upon waking. He is a pianist in a regional orchestra and finds his symptoms are affecting his ability to perform as well as before. His past medical history consists of mild asthma as a child, but he has otherwise been well with no recent illnesses.

On examination, there are visible deformities to his metacarpophalangeal joints associated with palpable tenderness. His wrists are mildly swollen. There are no skin or nail changes.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is associated with the worst prognosis?
explanation:
Anti-CCP antibodies are a marker of poor prognosis in rheumatoid arthritis

This patient has a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis a symmetrical, polyarthritis characterised by early morning joint pain and stiffness. Clinical features associated with a poor prognosis include positive anti-CCP antibodies and positive rheumatoid factor. Anti-CCP antibodies are usually seen in association with positive rheumatoid factor and the two together are strong predictors of early transformation from transient to persistent synovitis.

An insidious onset of symptoms is associated with a poor prognosis for rheumatoid arthritis rather than an acute onset of symptoms.

Female sex is associated with a poor prognosis of rheumatoid arthritis rather than male sex.

HLA-B27 is not associated with rheumatoid arthritis. It is associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as psoriatic and reactive arthritis.

question: A 54-year-old man is diagnosed as having gout. You are discussing ways to help prevent future attacks. Which one of the following is most likely to precipitate an attack of gout?

A 55-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with sudden onset severe pain, redness, and swelling in his right big toe, which started overnight. He has a history of hypertension and obesity but no previous similar episodes. Examination reveals erythema, warmth, and tenderness over the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The joint aspiration shows negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light microscopy.

Which is the most appropriate long-term management strategy for this patient?
options: Advise lifestyle modifications only and reassess if symptoms recur
Prescribing allopurinol after the acute attack has resolved
Prescribing colchicine daily for long-term prophylaxis
Starting allopurinol immediately alongside treatment for the acute attack
Use NSAIDs intermittently for future flare-ups without urate-lowering therapy
correctText: Prescribing allopurinol after the acute attack has resolved
explanation:
Offer allopurinol to all patients after their first attack of gout

Prescribing allopurinol after the acute attack has resolved

is correct because current guidelines recommend offering urate-lowering therapy (ULT) to all patients after their first attack of gout, regardless of symptom recurrence, to prevent future flares and long-term joint damage. Allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is the first-line ULT and should be started after the acute attack has fully resolved, as initiating it during an active flare may worsen or prolong the attack. The crystal-confirmed gout makes allopurinol the most appropriate long-term management option.

Advise lifestyle modifications only and reassess if symptoms recur

is incorrect because while lifestyle modifications (e.g., weight loss, reducing alcohol and purine intake, staying hydrated) are beneficial, they are not sufficient alone to prevent future gout attacks. Allopurinol should be initiated after the first gout attack, as many patients will have recurrent attacks, and untreated hyperuricemia increases the risk of chronic gouty arthritis and tophi formation.

Prescribing colchicine daily for long-term prophylaxis

is incorrect because although low-dose colchicine can be used for short-term prophylaxis (6 months) when starting urate-lowering therapy, it is not a substitute for allopurinol in the long-term management of gout. Colchicine helps reduce acute flare-ups but does not lower uric acid levels or prevent joint damage.

Starting allopurinol immediately alongside treatment for the acute attack

is incorrect because initiating allopurinol during an active gout attack can trigger or prolong the flare due to fluctuations in uric acid levels. The best approach is to first control the acute inflammation with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids, then start allopurinol 2 weeks after symptom resolution to prevent further attacks.

Use NSAIDs intermittently for future flare-ups without urate-lowering therapy

is incorrect because while NSAIDs are effective for acute gout management, they do not address the underlying hyperuricemia and do not prevent joint damage from recurrent attacks. Urate-lowering therapy should be offered after the first attack to reduce long-term complications.

question:
A 35-year-old man presents to his GP with longstanding recurrent oral and genital ulceration. He has no past medical history. He is from Turkey.

On examination, there is ulceration of the mouth and genital region. Synovitis of both wrists is noted along with a violaceous rash on the shins.

What is the HLA association with the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Behcet's syndrome is associated with HLA B51

HLA B51

is correct. The patient likely has Behcet's disease given his recurrent oral and genital ulceration. Other features of this condition include rashes e.g. erythema nodosum and arthritis in some cases. It is common among people from the Silk Road region e.g. Turkey. It is associated with HLA B27.

HLA B27

is incorrect. This is associated with ankylosing spondylitis. The absence of back pain makes this unlikely.

HLA DQ2

is incorrect. This is associated with coeliac disease. This can cause arthritis but would also likely cause gastrointestinal symptoms, which are absent.

HLA DR4

is incorrect. This is associated with rheumatoid arthritis. While this can cause synovitis it would be unlikely to cause recurrent ulceration or erythema nodosum.

HLA DRB1

is incorrect. This has been implicated in systemic lupus erythematosus. This can cause synovitis and oral ulceration. However, it is unlikely to cause genital ulceration and is more common in women.

question:
A 66-year-old woman attends the clinic with weakness and muscle pain. On examination, you note a proximal muscle weakness of the upper (MRC grade 4/5) and lower (MRC grade 3/5) limbs. You also note a bilateral lilac discolouration of the eyelids with swelling of the eyelids and skin around the eyes.

What antibody is most specific to the underlying condition?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis is associated with the anti-Jo-1 antibody

The patient most likely has a diagnosis of dermatomyositis as indicated by the proximal muscle weakness and heliotrope rash. Polymyositis and dermatomyositis are autoimmune disorders where there is inflammation in the muscles (myositis). Polymyositis is a condition of chronic inflammation of muscles. Dermatomyositis is a connective tissue disorder where there is a chronic inflammation of the skin and muscles. The presence of cutaneous manifestations, in this case, favours a diagnosis of dermatomyositis.

Anti-Jo-1 antibody

is correct.  Although this antibody is not particularly sensitive to dermatomyositis, it is highly specific, making this the best answer.  Antibodies to Jo1 are found in 20-60% of patients with primary polymyositis or dermatomyositis and less commonly in association with other connective tissue disease. Anti-Jo1 positive patients tend to have the poorest prognosis with more prominent lung involvement and less skin involvement

Anti dsDNA

is incorrect. The anti-double stranded DNA antibodies (anti-dsDNA) are considered a specific marker for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Although muscle weakness can occur in SLE, the presence of the heliotrope rash favours a diagnosis of dermatomyositis. Furthermore, the absence of other diagnostic criteria of SLE (e.g. oral ulcers, fever, and neurological dysfunction) makes it a less likely diagnosis.

Anti-PL-7 antibody

is incorrect. Although this can be positive in dermatomyositis, it is not sensitive nor specific to this condition.

Anti-Smith

is incorrect. Anti-Smith antibody is another highly specific antibody for SLE.

Antinuclear antibody

(ANA) is incorrect. Although ANA is a relatively sensitive test, with the majority of patients (around 80%) being positive, it is not specific to dermatomyositis.

question: Which one of the following is least recognised in polyarteritis nodosa?

A 50-year-old man plays tennis 5 times a week at his local club. He attends his GP surgery for elbow pain. He has taken ibuprofen regularly for the last 4 weeks. Tenderness is greatest over the lateral epicondyle.

Given the likely diagnosis, which movement would reproduce the pain when the elbow is in the extended position?
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis: worse on resisted wrist extension/suppination whilst elbow extended

This patient is experiencing tennis elbow or lateral epicondylitis. It is typical for there to be focal tenderness as reported in the question. The tendon most affected is extensor carpi radials brevis. The question is in recognition of this. Playing tennis has overworked the tendon and led to the pain. The correct answer is wrist extension. The other answers do not involve the wrist extensor tendon.

question:
A 48-year-old woman presents with dysphagia, reflux and skin stiffening. On examination, she has scleroderma and telangiectasias affecting the chest and shoulders and is hypertensive with a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg. She is found to have anti-scl-70 antibodies as well as anti-nuclear antibodies.

Which of the following is the most common cause of death in patients with her condition?
explanation:
The most common cause of death in systemic sclerosis is respiratory involvement:

The prognosis for diffuse systemic sclerosis is poor. Death mainly occurs from respiratory involvement, especially pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), which can lead to right-sided heart failure. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is another leading cause of death. Other respiratory complications include pulmonary haemorrhage, pneumonia (see below) and pneumothorax.

Cardiac calcification is a broad term for any calcification affecting the valves, coronary arteries, or the heart muscle itself. It is usually due to coronary artery disease, and it is not a prominent feature in systemic sclerosis.

Oesophageal dysmotility can cause dysphagia, oesophageal reflux, atypical chest pain and aspiration pneumonia. It is not the leading cause of death in systemic sclerosis, although aspiration pneumonia is an important respiratory complication in this cohort.

Renal disease can be a feature of systemic sclerosis but is not the leading cause of death. The most serious renal manifestation is scleroderma renal crisis, which occurs in a minority of patients (around 5%) and is characterised by malignant hypertension and oligo/anuric acute renal failure.

Similarly, hypertension can occur, usually as a result of renal damage, and this patient is indeed hypertensive; however, this is not the leading cause of death in these patients.

question:
A 76-year-old female presents with a 1 month history of left sided temporal headaches and jaw claudication. Biopsy of left temporal artery is negative.


Hb	130 g/l
Platelets	359 * 109/l
WBC	10 * 109/l
CRP	89 mg/l

What is the next best step in management?

A 58-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of painful swelling of the 1st metatarsophalangeal joint of his right foot. He has a history of hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and osteoarthritis. His list of medications includes amlodipine, ibuprofen, omeprazole, indapamide and atorvastatin.

Which of his list of medications is most likely to have precipitated his acute attack of gout?
explanation:
Thiazide diuretics can precipitate an attack of gout

Thiazide diuretics, such as indapamide, chlortalidone and bendroflumethiazide, can precipitate an acute attack of gout by reducing renal excretion of uric acid. The other drugs are less associated.

question: You are the ST1 working in the rheumatology out-patient clinic. Your next patient is a 25-year-old man who was diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) 12 months ago. Despite regular physiotherapy and trials of two different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) he remains symptomatic and asks you about the potential benefits of TNF-inhibitor therapy. You should tell him that TNF-inhibitors will improve all of the following except:

A 44-year-old woman presents with painful joints.

She says the joints in her hands are becoming stiff, swollen, and painful. The stiffness is worse in the mornings.

On examination, some of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands are swollen. They are tender to palpate and there is a reduced range of movement in the fingers.

Relevant bloods are shown below:


Hb	110 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	456 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	10.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
CRP	34 mg/L	(< 5)
Rheumatoid factor	Positive
Anti-CCP	Positive

Given the most likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
options: Dual DMARD therapy with bridging steroids
Single DMARD therapy with bridging steroids
TNF-α inhibitor and single DMARD combination therapy
correctText: Single DMARD therapy with bridging steroids
explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis: initial management is conventional DMARD monotherapy (usually methotrexate), often with short-term bridging corticosteroid

Single DMARD therapy with bridging steroids

is correct. This patient's signs, symptoms, and blood results suggest a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. The current recommendation is that early DMARD monotherapy should be used, usually with steroids to control symptoms whilst the DMARD is initiated, as steroids act faster than the DMARDs.

Dual DMARD therapy with bridging steroids

is incorrect. This patient's signs, symptoms, and blood results suggest a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. The current evidence suggests that early DMARD

monotherapy

should be used, usually with steroids to control symptoms whilst the DMARD is initiated. Combination therapy may be used if the patient has not responded to monotherapy at 3 months.

High dose oral tapering steroids

is incorrect. In rheumatoid arthritis, steroids are used either as bridging to reduce symptoms whilst the DMARD is initiated or as treatment of acute flares. Management of a new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis does not consist of steroids alone, and bridging doses used are generally low (less than 10mg prednisolone per day). This answer is therefore incorrect.

Paracetamol and topical NSAIDs

is incorrect. This is the first-line treatment for osteoarthritis, particularly in the hands or knees. The patient in this case, however, is suffering from rheumatoid arthritis. The early morning stiffness, proximal interphalangeal joint/metacarpophalangeal joint involvement, and blood results suggest rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis.

TNF-α inhibitor and single DMARD combination therapy

is incorrect. TNF-α inhibitors may be used in rheumatoid arthritis if the patient does not respond to the DMARD monotherapy within 3 months.

question: Looser's zones x-ray are most characteristically associated with which one of the following conditions?

You see a 70-year-old male patient with back pain. He says he has had lower back pain for about 12 months which is slowly getting worse. It now radiates to his buttocks, thighs and legs bilaterally (but his left leg is worse than the right). He describes the pain as 'cramping' and 'burning'. He says that when he walks for more than a few minutes his legs become weak and numb. If he sits down and leans forward the symptoms go. He finds standing exacerbates the symptoms. He is worried as he is losing his independence as he does not feel stable on his feet, he now has a walking aid. His wife thinks he has a more stooped posture than 12 months ago.

His past medical history includes tablet controlled hypertension. He has never smoked and has a normal BMI.

On examination, he has a wide-based gate. Neurological examination of his lower limbs is normal. His peripheral pulses feel normal.

What diagnosis is most likely given the presentation and examination findings?
explanation:
Spinal stenosis is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with gradual onset leg and back pain, weakness and numbness which is brought on by walking (with a normal clinical examination)

This man's presentation is most consistent with a diagnosis of spinal stenosis. Spinal stenosis typically presents with gradual onset leg and back pain, weakness and numbness which is brought on by walking. Patients often say that the pain is relieved by sitting and leaning forward and is better if walking up a hill. Physical examination findings are frequently normal in patients with lumbar spinal stenosis. Therefore, the correct answer is 2.

The main differential diagnosis is vascular claudication but he has normal pulses peripherally. Therefore, option 4 is wrong.

Sciatica is more likely to present with unilateral leg pain. Therefore, option 3 is incorrect.

Non-specific lower back pain is common but does not present with lower limb symptoms. Therefore, option 5 is wrong.

question:
A 44-year-old woman presents to her GP with an aching pain in the radial aspect of her forearm. It has been present for several weeks.

On examination, there is tenderness on the radial aspect of the forearm about 5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle. Pain is notably worse on pronation of the forearm. Movements of the thumb do not affect the pain.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Radial tunnel syndrome presents similarly to lateral epicondylitis however pain is typically distal to the epicondyle and worse on elbow extension/forearm pronation

Radial tunnel syndrome

is correct. Radial tunnel syndrome describes a mononeuropathy of the posterior interosseous nerve within the radial tunnel. Key features are tenderness maximal at a point 5cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, and the pain is worse on forearm pronation. Pronation of the forearm can increase tension in the radial tunnel and exacerbate nerve compression - a finding characteristic of radial tunnel syndrome.

Carpal tunnel syndrome

is incorrect. Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve at the wrist. Pain is felt in the hand, accompanied by sensory loss and paraesthesia in the median nerve distribution. These symptoms are not described here, so this answer is incorrect.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis

is incorrect. In de Quervain's tenosynovitis, there is a thickening of the tendon sheaths around the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons along the radial styloid at the wrist. The cardinal features are pain over the radial aspect of the wrist, exacerbated by thumb movement and radial or ulnar deviation of the wrist. In this case, movements of the thumb do not affect the pain, making De Quervain's tenosynovitis less likely. The site of tenderness described in this patient is not in keeping with de Quervain's tenosynovitis. Finkelstein's test is often used to help diagnose this condition by exacerbating pain with thumb movement and ulnar deviation.

Golfer's elbow

is incorrect. Golfer's elbow is also known as medial epicondylitis. Pain in this condition is felt over the medical aspect of the elbow and forearm, and tenderness is elicited over the medial epicondyle. The patient, in this case, has pain over the lateral aspect of the forearm, making this answer incorrect.

Student's elbow

is incorrect. This is seen following prolonged pressure on the elbows (e.g. from studying a textbook), and results in swelling/pain behind the olecranon. This patient has tenderness over the radial aspect of the forearm 5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, a key feature of radial tunnel syndrome rather than the student's elbow.

question:
A 38-year-old Vietnamese man presents to the emergency department with a 3-week history of left-sided flank pain. He denies urinary symptoms. He had a course of nitrofurantoin prescribed by his GP which has not helped. On examination, he is febrile at 38.4 °C, and extension of his left hip worsens his pain.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fever/back pain with pain on extension of the hip → iliopsoas abscess

The persistent flank pain, fever and examination findings point towards an iliopsoas abscess. You can also expect to see a limp when the patient walks. These can be divided into primary and secondary causes.

Pott's disease is a form of tuberculosis that occurs outside the lungs whereby disease is seen in the vertebrae. It would fit with back pain and fever, but the distinctive examination findings point towards an iliopsoas abscess.

You would not expect to see constitutional symptoms such as fever in mechanical back pain.

Pyelonephritis is an important differential to bear in mind, but the examination findings are more suggestive of an iliopsoas abscess. It would be useful to exclude this by getting a urine dip and an ultrasound.

Kidney stones are incredibly painful and may produce fever if they become infected. Given the duration of his symptoms, this option is less likely.

question: Which one of the following best describes rheumatoid factor?
options: IgG against the Fc portion of IgM
IgM against the Fc portion of IgA
IgM against the Fc portion of IgM
IgM against the Fc portion of IgG
IgG against the Fc portion of IgA
correctText: IgM against the Fc portion of IgG
explanation:
Rheumatoid factor is an IgM antibody against IgG

The correct answer is

IgM against the Fc portion of IgG

. Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an autoantibody that is classically associated with rheumatoid arthritis, though it can be present in other autoimmune conditions and even in some healthy individuals. RF is predominantly an IgM antibody that targets the Fc (fragment crystallisable) region of IgG antibodies. This creates immune complexes that can deposit in joints and other tissues, contributing to the inflammatory process seen in rheumatoid arthritis. RF is detected in approximately 70-80% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, making it a useful diagnostic marker, though not specific to the condition.

IgG against the Fc portion of IgM

is incorrect. While IgG autoantibodies do exist in autoimmune conditions, rheumatoid factor specifically refers to antibodies targeting IgG, not IgM. Additionally, the classic RF is predominantly of the IgM isotype, not IgG. This configuration would represent a different type of autoantibody altogether.

IgM against the Fc portion of IgA

is incorrect. Rheumatoid factor targets IgG, not IgA. While anti-IgA antibodies can exist in certain conditions, such as IgA deficiency, they are not classified as rheumatoid factor. The interaction between IgM and IgA does not play a significant role in the pathophysiology of rheumatoid arthritis.

IgM against the Fc portion of IgM

is incorrect. This would represent an autoantibody against the same immunoglobulin class, which is not the definition of rheumatoid factor. While autoantibodies against various self-antigens can occur in autoimmune diseases, RF specifically refers to antibodies (primarily IgM) that target the Fc portion of IgG.

IgG against the Fc portion of IgA

is incorrect. This describes an IgG autoantibody targeting IgA, which is not rheumatoid factor. While less common forms of RF can include IgG and IgA isotypes that target IgG, the classic and predominant form of RF is IgM antibodies targeting the Fc portion of IgG. Anti-IgA antibodies are associated with different clinical scenarios, such as transfusion reactions in IgA-deficient individuals.

question:
A 66-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with six months of exertional right knee pain. She has a past medical history of obesity and type 2 diabetes. She takes metformin.

On examination, there is crepitus when examining the right knee. There is no swelling.

Given the most likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate initial step?
explanation:
Knee osteoarthritis - topical NSAIDs are first-line

Topical ibuprofen

is correct. This patient presents with activity-related knee pain and on examination there is crepitus. Obesity, female sex, and age are risk factors for knee osteoarthritis (OA), which is the most likely underlying cause here. The first line of pharmacological treatment is a topical NSAID.

Intra-articular steroid injection

is incorrect. Some patients find that steroid injections give them temporary relief from symptoms of OA. However, they should usually be used after the failure of topical or oral medical treatment.

Oral codeine

is incorrect. Similar to paracetamol, this is only advised if used infrequently for short-term pain relief and all other pharmacological treatments are contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective.

Oral ibuprofen

is incorrect. If topical NSAIDs are insufficient then oral NSAIDs are recommended next. Gastroprotection should be provided.

Oral paracetamol

is incorrect. This was previously recommended as a first-line treatment for OA but is no longer advised in this manner. It is only recommended if used infrequently for short-term pain relief and all other pharmacological treatments are contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective.

question:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the paediatric outpatient clinic by his parents due to delayed walking and swelling at both wrists. He has been exclusively breastfed and spends little time outdoors. On examination, there is bilateral widening of the wrist joints and mild bowing of the lower limbs. Laboratory investigations reveal:


Calcium	1.95 mmol/L	(2.20 - 2.60)
Phosphate	0.8 mmol/L	(1.3 - 2.1)
Alkaline phosphatase	900 IU/L	(110 - 320)
25-hydroxyvitamin D	10 nmol/L	(>50)

Which pathological process most likely explains the wrist findings?
options: Excess unmineralised osteoid at growth plate
Defective collagen synthesis in bone matrix
Impaired endochondral ossification due to cartilage enzyme defect
Reduced osteoblast activity from genetic mutation
correctText: Excess unmineralised osteoid at growth plate
explanation:
Rickets can present as widening of the wrist joints due to an excess of non-mineralized osteoid at the growth plate

Excess unmineralised osteoid at growth plate

is correct because rickets results from inadequate mineralisation of bone during childhood, usually due to vitamin D deficiency as seen in this case (low vitamin D, hypocalcaemia, raised alkaline phosphatase). This leads to an accumulation of non-mineralised osteoid at sites of active growth—especially the metaphyses near the wrist—causing widening and swelling of these joints. Understanding this pathophysiology is essential for recognising classic clinical signs such as wrist widening or 'rickety rosary' on the chest.

Increased osteoclastic bone resorption

would be more characteristic of conditions like hyperparathyroidism or Paget's disease, where excessive breakdown of bone predominates rather than impaired mineralisation per se. In rickets, although there may be some secondary parathyroid hormone elevation, the primary issue is failure to mineralise new bone.

Defective collagen synthesis in bone matrix

refers to disorders like osteogenesis imperfecta, which present with brittle bones and frequent fractures but not with widened wrists or metaphyseal cupping typical of rickets.

Impaired endochondral ossification due to cartilage enzyme defect

describes skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia or hypophosphatasia; these do cause abnormal growth plates but are not associated with biochemical evidence of vitamin D deficiency or classical radiological/clinical features seen here.

Reduced osteoblast activity from genetic mutation

might occur in rare inherited forms of osteoporosis (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta type VI), but would not explain the combination of low vitamin D, raised alkaline phosphatase and typical clinical presentation as seen in this scenario.

question: A 27-year-old woman presents with painful genital ulceration. She has had recurrent attacks for the past four years. Oral aciclovir has had little effect on the duration of her symptoms. She has also noticed for the past year almost weekly attacks of mouth ulcers which again are slow to heal. Her only past medical history of note is being treated for thrombophlebitis two years ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 29-year-old with adult onset Still's comes to the rheumatology clinic for review. She still has significant symptoms including joint pains and a persistent skin rash despite methotrexate and etanercept. Examination reveals a macular erythematous rash and active synovitis. CRP is elevated at 95 mg/l.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?

A 57-year-old woman presents with a three month history of right-sided hip pain. This seems to have come on spontaneously without any obvious precipitating event. The pain is described as being worse on the 'outside' of the hip and is particularly bad at night when she lies on the right hand side.

On examination there is a full range of movement in the hip including internal and external rotation. Deep palpation of the lateral aspect of the right hip joint recreates the pain.

An x-ray of the right hip is reported as follows:


Right hip: Minor narrowing of the joint space otherwise normal appearance

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 39-year-old woman is seen in the rheumatology clinic having originally presented with a progressive history of skin plaques and guttate lesions. On presentation, she had also developed swelling and pain of the distal fingers and toes and nail thickening and pitting.

Initial treatment did not slow the progression of her condition and therefore the rheumatologist recommends commencing apremilast. This treatment is known to suppress pro-inflammatory mediators synthesis and promote anti-inflammatory mediators.

What type of medication has been recommended?
explanation:
Apremilast: phosphodiesterase type-4 (PDE4) inhibitor

This patient has presented with features in keeping with the seronegative spondyloarthropathy psoriatic arthritis. Treatment for the condition is based on severity with some patients only requiring simple nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and skin emollients for symptom control. Frequently however patients require other agents such as biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) (e.g. TNF-α inhibitors), conventional synthetic DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate), and

phosphodiesterase type-4 (PDE4) inhibitors

(e.g. apremilast). By inhibiting the dominant inflammatory enzyme in psoriatic arthritis, PDE4, apremilast down-regulates the expression of pro-inflammatory factors.

Alkylating agents

are typically used in the management of malignancies however certain examples such as cyclophosphamide can be used in autoimmune conditions when other medications have failed. These agents have a limited role in the management of psoriatic arthritis.

Antimetabolites

such as methotrexate are part of the DMARDs group of therapies and are often used in conditions such as psoriatic arthritis. Apremilast is a phosphodiesterase type-4 (PDE4) inhibitor, not an antimetabolite.

Cytotoxic antibiotics

are predominantly used as chemotherapy agents and have a limited role in the management of autoimmune conditions such as psoriatic arthritis.

Monoclonal antibodies

such as ustekinumab and secukinumab are frequently used as second-line therapy in psoriatic arthritis. Apremilast is not a monoclonal antibody.

question:
A 45-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with back pain radiating to his right leg. He has no past medical history and does not take any regular medications.

On examination, there is sensory loss on the posterolateral aspect of the right leg and lateral aspect of the foot. There is a weakness of plantar flexion and a reduced ankle reflex.

What nerve root is most likely to be affected?
explanation:
S1 lesion features = Sensory loss of posterolateral aspect of leg and lateral aspect of foot,  weakness in plantar flexion of foot, reduced ankle reflex, positive sciatic nerve stretch test

S1

is the right answer. The patient presents with low back pain radiating to his leg, suggesting radiculopathy. The distribution of sensory findings, weakness of plantar flexion and reduced ankle reflex suggests an S1 lesion.

L3

is incorrect. Involvement of this nerve root would cause sensory loss over the anterior thigh and a weak quadriceps. The femoral stretch test may be positive and the knee reflex reduced.

L4

is incorrect. Involvement of this nerve root would cause sensory loss over the anterior knee, a weak quadriceps and reduced knee reflex.

L5

is incorrect. Involvement of this nerve root would cause weakness of the foot and big toe dorsiflexion. The reflexes would be intact.  The sciatic stretch test may be positive.

T10

is incorrect. Injury to a nerve root at T10 would not cause pain radiating down the leg.

question:
A 26-year-old renal transplant recipient secondary to polycystic kidney disease enters the follow-up clinic. She has been started on multiple immunosuppressant agents including mycophenolate mofetil.

What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation:
Mycophenolate mofetil inhibits of inosine-5'-monophosphate dehydrogenase which is needed for purine synthesis

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) reduces lymphocyte production through inhibition of iosine-5'-monophosphate dehydrogenase. It is typically used in organ transplantation and autoimmune conditions. Both MMF and azathioprine inhibit purine synthesis but through different mechanisms.

Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus and ciclosporin) are immunosuppressants which work through reducing t-cell differentiation.

Protease inhibitors such as ritonavir and darunavir are antivirals used against HIV and hepatitis.

Statins are examples of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. They work by reducing LDL cholesterol.

Hydroxycarbamide is an example of a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor which decreases the production of deoxyribonucleotides reducing DNA synthesis. It is used to treat cancers.

question: Patients with Sjogren's syndrome are at an increased risk of which one of the following malignancies?
explanation:
Patients with Sjogren's syndrome have an increased risk of lymphoid malignancies

The correct answer is

Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma

. Sjogren's syndrome, an autoimmune condition characterised by dry eyes and mouth, has been associated with an increased risk of lymphoproliferative disorders. This includes Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma which is the most common malignancy in these patients. The exact reason for this association is not entirely clear but it could be related to ongoing immune stimulation leading to clonal expansion and eventually malignant transformation.

Myeloma

is a malignancy of plasma cells in the bone marrow. While there are certain risk factors such as age, race, family history and certain genetic changes that can increase one's risk of myeloma, there is no established link between Sjogren's syndrome and an increased risk of developing myeloma.

Oesophageal cancer

has several known risk factors including gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), obesity, smoking and heavy alcohol use. There is no strong evidence to suggest a direct link between Sjogren's syndrome and oesophageal cancer.

Intraocular melanoma

, a rare form of eye cancer, also does not have a proven association with Sjogren's syndrome. Known risk factors include fair skin, light eye colour, increasing age and certain inherited skin conditions but not autoimmune diseases like Sjogren's syndrome.

Finally, while

Squamous cell skin cancer

can occur in patients with compromised immune systems such as organ transplant recipients or those with HIV/AIDS, there isn't sufficient evidence to suggest an increased risk in patients with Sjogren's Syndrome specifically.

question:
A 65-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with pain in his hands, which is worse with activity and at the end of the day. He has a past medical history of psoriasis. He does not take any regular medications.

On examination, there were bony swellings of 3 distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints on both hands.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Swelling at the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) is a feature of osteoarthritis in the hand

Osteoarthritis

is the correct answer. Bony swelling of the DIP joints is known as Heberden's nodes. Pain worse with activity (rather than rest) is more characteristic of OA than inflammatory arthritis.

Psoriatic arthritis

is incorrect. This can cause swelling of the DIP joints. However, the swelling is more likely to be boggy rather than bony in inflammatory arthritis. Additionally, the pain of inflammatory arthritis tends to be worse in the morning and improves with activity.

Reactive arthritis

is incorrect. This tends to cause a large joint lower limb oligoarthritis rather than a DIP predominant arthritis. There is also no history of recent infection.

Rheumatoid arthritis

is incorrect. This does not affect the DIP joints.

Systemic lupus erythematosus

is incorrect. This typically affects the MCP and PIPs joints and is usually associated with some other evidence of systemic autoimmune disease, which is not present in this case.

question:
A 52-male presented with intermitted fever, malaise, and arthralgia in his knees and hands. These symptoms had been on-going for the last 8 weeks. He has also noted frank haematuria on 5 occasions over the last week and a mottled lace-like discolouration of his skin on both his legs.

Observation and blood tests are as follows:


Blood pressure	128/82 mmHg
Heart rate	86 bpm
Temperature	37.8 deg C
Respiratory rate	12 /min
oxygen saturation	96 %


Hb	136 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Platelets	398 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	10 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Urea	7.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	150 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	50 mg/L	(< 5)
HBsAg	positive
Anti-HBs	negative
Anti-HBc	positive
p-ANCA	positive
c-ANCA	negative

What neurological disorder is associated with the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa can cause a mononeuritis multiplex syndrome

The patient's symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgia, frank haematuria, livedo reticularis (mottled lace-like discolouration of skin), raised inflammatory markers, poor renal function, positive hepatitis B serology, and positive perinuclear-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA) point to a diagnosis of polyarthritis nodosa (PAN). PAN is a vasculitis affecting medium-sized arteries with necrotizing inflammation leading to aneurysm formation. PAN is more common in middle-aged men and is associated with mononeuritis multiplex and sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

Mononeuritis multiplex is a painful, asymmetrical, asynchronous sensory and motor peripheral neuropathy involving isolated damage to at least 2 separate nerve areas. Multiple nerves in random areas of the body can be affected. Other causes include diabetes mellitus, sarcoidosis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Amyotrophy is a nerve disorder that is a complication of diabetes mellitus. It affects the thighs, hips, buttocks and legs, causing pain and muscle wasting.

Lambert-Eaton syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterized by muscle weakness of the limbs. Around 60% of those with Lambert-Eaton syndrome have an underlying malignancy, most commonly small-cell lung cancer. Antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels decrease the amount of calcium that can enter the presynaptic nerve ending, resulting in less acetylcholine being released from the neuromuscular junction which causes muscle weakness. In contrast to myasthenia gravis, the muscle weakness will improve with activity.

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is characterized by degeneration of the dorsal columns and the lateral columns of the spinal cord due to demyelination. It is a neurological complication of vitamin B12 deficiency. It commonly presents with sensory deficits (loss of proprioception and vibration sense), paraesthesia, weakness, ataxia, and gait disturbance.

Syringomyelia ('syrinx' for short) is a collection of cerebrospinal fluid within the spinal canal. The classical presentation is a loss of temperature and pain sensation in a cape-like distribution (neck and arms), but preservation of light touch, proprioception and vibration. This is due to the crossing spinothalamic tracts in the anterior commissure of the spinal cord being the first tracts to be affected. Other symptoms and signs include spastic weakness (predominantly of the upper limbs), paraesthesia, neuropathic pain, and upgoing plantar reflexes, as well as bowel and bladder dysfunction.

question:
A 77-year-old woman is reviewed on the orthogeriatrics ward round 5 days following a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. The consultant decides to start her on a RANK ligand inhibitor for secondary prevention of osteoporosis.

Which of the following medications will you commence?
explanation:
Denosumab - RANKL inhibitor

Denosumab is is a human monoclonal antibody that is used in the treatment of osteoporosis. It prevents the development of osteoclasts by inhibiting RANKL. Osteoclasts break down bone, and therefore by preventing their development, bone loss is reduced.

It is given as a subcutaneous injection every six months.  It can also be given as a larger dose to prevent pathological fractures in patients with bone metastases from solid organ malignancy.

As bone breakdown is reduced by denosumab, hypocalcaemia is a potential side effect. All patients should have vitamin D levels checked (and replaced if necessary) prior to starting treatment to help to prevent this.

Raloxifene is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM) which can be used in the management of osteoporosis.  However, it is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Bisphosphonates, such alendronate or risedronate are used first line in osteoporosis in the majority of cases.

Teriparatide is a recombinant form of parathyroid hormone, which can also be used in the management of osteoporosis.

Aromatase inhibitors, such as letrozole, are used in the treatment of hormone-dependent breast cancers.

question: A 47-year-old female presents with elbow pain. She has just spent the weekend painting the house. On examination there is localised pain around the lateral epicondyle and a diagnosis of lateral epicondylitis is suspected. Which one of the following movements would characteristically worsen the pain?
options: Pronation of the forearm with the elbow flexed
Resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended
correctText: Resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended
explanation:
Lateral epicondylitis: worse on resisted wrist extension/suppination whilst elbow extended

The correct answer is

Resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended

. Lateral epicondylitis, also known as tennis elbow, is a condition characterised by pain and tenderness over the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. It occurs due to degeneration or damage to the common extensor tendon that originates from the lateral epicondyle, particularly affecting the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) muscle. The pain in lateral epicondylitis is aggravated by activities that involve wrist extension against resistance, especially when the elbow is in full extension.

Resisted thumb flexion

would not typically worsen the pain in lateral epicondylitis as it primarily involves the flexor pollicis longus and flexor pollicis brevis muscles, which are not associated with the common extensor tendon.

Thumb extension

does involve some of the extensor muscles of the forearm; however, it specifically targets the extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis muscles rather than those primarily affected in lateral epicondylitis.

Flexion of the elbow

involves contraction of biceps brachii and brachialis muscles while relaxing forearm extensors. Therefore, it would not be expected to exacerbate pain in lateral epicondylitis.

Pronation of the forearm with the elbow flexed

primarily activates pronator teres and pronator quadratus muscles. Although these movements may engage some components of common extensor tendon function, they do not specifically stress or aggravate it like resisted wrist extension with an extended elbow does.

question: A 45-year-old man who is known to have haemochromatosis presents with a swollen and painful right knee. An x-ray shows no fracture but extensive chondrocalcinosis. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following is most likely to present in the joint fluid?
explanation:
Pseudogout - weakly positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals

The correct answer is

Positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals

. In a patient with haemochromatosis and chondrocalcinosis, the likely diagnosis is calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease or pseudogout. The characteristic finding in joint fluid analysis in CPPD disease is the presence of positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals. These crystals are formed due to the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate in the joint cartilage, leading to inflammation and pain.

The first option,

Raised hyaluronic acid levels

, is not specific to any particular type of arthritis. Hyaluronic acid is a normal component of synovial fluid that provides lubrication and shock absorption. Its levels can be increased or decreased in various arthritic conditions but would not be diagnostic for CPPD disease.

The second option,

Monosodium urate crystals

, are associated with gout rather than pseudogout. Gout is caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals within joints, leading to an inflammatory response and acute attacks of arthritis. Although both gout and pseudogout can present with similar symptoms, their underlying pathophysiology and crystal types are different.

The third option,

Bipyramidal oxalate crystals

, are typically found in patients with primary hyperoxaluria or oxalosis, which results from excessive production or ingestion of oxalic acid. This condition can lead to kidney stones and systemic deposition of calcium oxalate crystals but would not cause chondrocalcinosis or pseudogout-like symptoms.

The fourth option,

Negatively birefringent calcium carbonate crystals

, does not correspond to any known pathological process in joint diseases. Calcium carbonate crystals do not typically form in the joint space, and their presence would not be expected in a patient with haemochromatosis and chondrocalcinosis.

question: A 54-year-old male presents with abdominal pain, testicular pain, weight loss, left foot drop and livedo reticularis. You suspect a diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa and request a full autoantibody screen. From the options given below, what are you most likely to see when the results of his autoantibody screen returns if the diagnosis is polyarteritis nodosa?
options: No autoantibody is likely to be positive
correctText: No autoantibody is likely to be positive

question:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic with a 6-month history of well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques on her cheeks and scalp. The lesions are worse after sun exposure. She has been using topical betamethasone 0.1% for 3 months with minimal improvement. Some areas on her scalp now show hair loss with scarring. She has no systemic symptoms. ANA is negative.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Discoid lupus erythematous - topical steroids → oral hydroxychloroquine

Oral hydroxychloroquine

is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient with discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) who has failed to respond adequately to topical steroids. The clinical presentation is classic for DLE with well-demarcated, erythematous, scaly plaques on sun-exposed areas (face and scalp), photosensitivity, and scarring alopecia. Antimalarials, particularly hydroxychloroquine, are considered the first-line systemic therapy for DLE when topical treatments are insufficient. Hydroxychloroquine typically works within 4-8 weeks and has a good safety profile with appropriate monitoring. The negative ANA is consistent with DLE, which often presents without systemic involvement or serological markers of systemic lupus erythematosus. Hydroxychloroquine not only treats the current lesions but may prevent new lesions and reduce photosensitivity.

Oral prednisolone

is not appropriate as first-line systemic therapy for DLE. Systemic corticosteroids are generally reserved for severe, rapidly progressive disease or when there are significant systemic features suggesting SLE. This patient has localized cutaneous disease without systemic symptoms. Long-term systemic steroids carry significant side effects including weight gain, diabetes, osteoporosis, and hypertension, making them unsuitable for chronic management of DLE.

Topical tacrolimus

could be considered as an alternative topical therapy, particularly for facial lesions where prolonged use of potent topical steroids may cause skin atrophy. However, this patient has already failed topical therapy for 3 months and has developed scarring alopecia, indicating that progression to systemic therapy is warranted rather than trying another topical agent.

Oral methotrexate

is typically considered a third-line agent for DLE after failure of antimalarials and is usually reserved for refractory cases. It has a more significant side effect profile including hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and teratogenicity, making it less suitable as a second-line agent in a young woman.

Phototherapy

is contraindicated in DLE as UV exposure can exacerbate the condition. The patient's history specifically mentions worsening after sun exposure, highlighting the photosensitive nature of her disease. Phototherapy could potentially trigger flares and lead to progression of the disease.

question: Potential complications of Paget's disease include each of the following except:

A 27-year-old female has been referred to the rheumatology clinic with gradually worsening joint stiffness in both her hands and wrists for the last 5 months. Blood tests done by her GP show a raised anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP).

On examination, she has a symmetrical polyarthritis affecting the proximal interphalangeal (PIP), metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and wrists.

Based on these features, which of these findings is most likely to be seen on plain radiography?
explanation:
Juxta-articular osteoporosis/osteopenia is an early x-ray feature of rheumatoid arthritis

This patient most likely has a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis based on her history, examination findings and blood results.

Typical radiographic features in early stages of the disease include loss of joint space, juxta-articular osteopenia/osteoporosis and soft tissue swelling. As the disease progresses, joint subluxation and periarticular erosions may be seen.

As this patient has only had symptoms for a relatively short period of time, it is more likely to see juxta-articular osteopenia, hence this is the correct option.

Chondrocalcinosis is a feature of systemic sclerosis.

Osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis are seen in osteoarthritis.

question:
A 27-year-old man is seen by his GP for polyarticular pain. He describes lower back, hip and finger pain and stiffness, which improves with movement throughout the day. He is currently undergoing physiotherapy for achilles tendonitis. On examination, his second and third finger digits are swollen and warm to touch maximally over the distal interphalangeal joints bilaterally. His second digit on the left hand is entirely swollen and inflamed despite no preceding trauma or evidence of infection.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Inflammatory arthritis involving DIP swelling and dactylitis points to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis

The condition being described is

psoriatic arthritis

, a seronegative arthropathy. Some of the key features described in this scenario are dactylitis, distal interphalangeal inflammation, sacroiliitis and achilles tendonitis. Associated psoriatic skin and nail changes correlate poorly with arthritis and often come later.

Ankylosing spondylitis

is the most tempting alternative answer. As in psoriatic arthritis, these patients often have sacroiliitis alongside complications such as achilles tendonitis, as in this scenario. However, dactylitis and digit inflammation are not typical of ankylosing spondylitis, so psoriatic arthritis is a better answer.

Rheumatoid arthritis

(RA) can also present with symmetrical polyarthritis affecting the hand joints. However, the metacarpophalangeal joints are more commonly affected in RA, unlike in this scenario. In addition, tendonitis and sacroiliitis are less common than in psoriatic arthritis, so it is an incorrect answer.

Enteropathic arthritis

is also a seronegative arthropathy but is an incorrect answer. While it can cause polyarticular arthritis, there is no mention of symptoms of underlying gastrointestinal disease, so it is a less likely diagnosis than psoriatic arthritis.

Reactive arthritis

can also cause tendonitis and arthritis. However, there is no mention of a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection trigger in the question, which makes this answer less likely.

question: Which one of the following statements regarding systemic lupus erythematous is true?
options: It is linked with HLA A5
Onset is typically between 20-40 years old
It is more common in Caucasians
The incidence has decreased in the past 30 years
correctText: Onset is typically between 20-40 years old

question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with three months of right wrist pain. She is finding it difficult to open jars. There is no history of trauma. She has recently given birth to her first child.

On clinical examination, there was minimal swelling on the dorsal wrist and she was tender in the region of the radial styloid. Pain was elicited in the dorsal thumb and wrist on applying longitudinal traction and ulnar deviation to the thumb. The neurovascular examination of the hand and wrist was normal.

Plain radiographs of the wrist were unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pain on the radial side of the wrist/tenderness over the radial styloid process ? De Quervain's tenosynovitis

Carpal tunnel syndrome is incorrect as this is more likely to be associated with neurological signs and symptoms such as weakness and sensory changes.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis is the correct answer. This condition typically affects women between 30-50 and is particularly associated with picking up young children. Clinical examination findings of tenderness near the radial styloid and a positive Finkelstein's test are suggestive.

Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with significant swelling, redness and pain and typically affects more than one joint.

The absence of trauma makes a scaphoid fracture unlikely.

Osteoarthritis is typically suggested by radiographic changes such as joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral cysts and sclerosis, which are absent in this case.

question:
A 29-year-old man presents to the rheumatology clinic. He has been experiencing a dull ache of his lower back, usually commencing on waking first thing in the morning and improving as the day goes on. He also reports significantly reduced movement of the entire spine, especially in the lumbar region.

The patient has also recently been diagnosed with anterior uveitis.

What investigation would be most appropriate to support the likely diagnosis?
options: Chest x-ray to identify apical fibrosis
explanation:
Diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis can be best supported by sacro-ilitis on a pelvic X-ray
