This is a classic case in keeping with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) with features including reduced spinal movement and stiffness affecting a younger patient (normal age of onset is 20-30 years). Symptoms typically are worse on awaking and ease throughout the day. Extra spinal features include anterior uveitis, aortitis, aortic valve insufficiency, and pulmonary fibrosis. Although there is no single test to confirm the diagnosis several investigations can be used to aid make the diagnosis. The most useful investigation to establish the diagnosis is a however a

pelvic x-ray to look for sacro-iliitis

. The presence of sacroiliitis is both a common feature in AS (even in the early stages of the condition) as well as being relatively specific for the diagnosis. Most other investigative findings either lack specificity, sensitivity or only develop late into the condition.

Although AS is one of only a few conditions that can result in pulmonary

apical fibrosis

it remains a rare extra-articular manifestation. Apical fibrosis also only develops late in the condition and therefore a chest x-ray is not a particularly useful test when investigating for the disease.

Bamboo spine

is a specific characteristic found in cases of AS where the spinal vertebral body fuses by the marginal syndesmophytes. The resultant fused spine resembles a bamboo tree trunk (hence the name) and causes extreme reduction of spinal movement. Although specific for AS, again, it is a very late sign and therefore is less useful for early diagnosis.

Serum ESR

, like most inflammatory markers, is typically raised in AS however, this is a very non-specific finding and therefore is not helpful when attempting to diagnose the condition.

Again, a

serum HLA-B27 level

is not particularly useful when diagnosis AS as, although it is positive in most AS patients, multiple other diseases are associated with the presence of this antigen. Serum HLA-B27 is also found in approximately 10% of the general population meaning it is neither a specific nor sensitive finding.

question:
A 41-year-old woman is reviewed in the oncology clinic, following a recent diagnosis of ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, for which she is receiving adjuvant treatment with tamoxifen. She reports that she has been feeling increasingly tired and weak recently.

On examination, there is a new, reddish-purple rash surrounding her eyelids. She also reveals symmetrical, violaceous papules over the dorsal aspect of her proximal and distal interphalangeal joints.

Which of the following auto-antibodies is most likely to be positive in this patient?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis antibodies: ANA most common, anti-Mi-2 most specific

This patient has a diagnosis of dermatomyositis - a paraneoplastic condition seen in the context of a range of solid and haematological malignancies, including breast cancer. This diagnosis is supported by the classic description of the 'heliotrope' rash around her eyelids, as well as Gottron's papules. Although the presence of fatigue and weakness is non-specific in patients with cancer, in this instance, it points towards the myopathic element of her condition. The most common antibodies found in patients with dermatomyositis are anti-nuclear antibodies, which are seen in 60% of patients.

Anti-Mi-2 antibodies are very specific for dermatomyositis but are only seen in around 25% of affected patients.

c-ANCA antibodies are associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). In GPA, associated rashes tend to be more purpuric in nature, and the clinical history is more likely to include features such as epistaxis or renal impairment.

Anti-Yo antibodies are seen in patients with breast cancer and paraneoplastic syndrome but tend to be associated with cerebellar degeneration and ataxia.

Rheumatoid factor is positive in around 5-10% of all patients, irrespective of diagnosis. It has also been found to be elevated in a minority of patients with dermatomyositis and other inflammatory myopathies but is much less likely to be raised than ANA in this patient.

question:
A 24-year-old woman presents to her GP with low back pain. She is otherwise fit and well. During her childhood, she reports a number of fractures of fingers and wrists. The patient explains that both her father and sister have had multiple fractures throughout their lives too.

On examination, she appears to have scoliosis and paralumbar tenderness. She has blue-grey sclera.

Given the likely diagnosis, a mutation in which type of collagen is responsible?
explanation:
Osteogenesis imperfecta occurs due to an abnormality in type 1 collagen

The diagnosis here is that of osteogenesis imperfecta, given the history of fractures, scoliosis presumably due to vertebral fractures, family history and examination findings. This is due to a mutation in type 1 collagen, which is the main component of the organic part of bone, as well as skin and tendons.

Type 2 collagen is the main component of cartilage. Chondrodysplasias may be caused by mutations in type 2 collagen.

Type 3 collagen is the main component of reticular fibres. Mutations in this may lead to a type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Type 4 collagen forms the basal lamina. Mutations in this may cause Alport's syndrome and Goodpasture's syndrome.

Type 5 collagen is found in cell surfaces, hair and placentas. Disorders include the classical variant of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

question: A 61-year-old man is noted to have thickened patches of skin over his knuckles and extensor surfaces consistent with Gottron's papules. His creatinine kinase levels are also elevated. A diagnosis of dermatomyositis is suspected. Which one of the following types of autoantibody is most specific for this condition?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis antibodies: ANA most common, anti-Mi-2 most specific

The correct answer is

Anti-Mi-2 antibodies

. Anti-Mi-2 antibodies are highly specific for dermatomyositis, a connective tissue disease characterized by muscle inflammation and skin manifestations such as Gottron's papules. The presence of these autoantibodies in the patient's serum supports the diagnosis of dermatomyositis.

In contrast,

Anti-scl-70 antibodies

are associated with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), a different connective tissue disease that primarily affects the skin and internal organs. While some patients with dermatomyositis might have overlapping features with scleroderma, anti-scl-70 antibodies are not specific for dermatomyositis.

Anti-Jo-1 antibodies

, also known as anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase antibodies, are found in patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, particularly polymyositis and dermatomyositis. Although they can be present in some cases of dermatomyositis, they are more commonly associated with the antisynthetase syndrome which is characterised by myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon and mechanic's hands. Therefore, anti-Jo-1 antibodies are not as specific for dermatomyositis compared to anti-Mi-2 antibodies.

Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs)

are a group of autoantibodies that target various nuclear components within cells. ANAs can be detected in various autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Sjogren's syndrome and mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD). Although ANAs may be present in patients with dermatomyositis or other connective tissue diseases, they lack specificity for any particular condition.

Lastly,

Anti-centromere bodies

, also known as anti-centromere antibodies, are associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (also known as CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly and Telangiectasia). These autoantibodies target the centromere proteins in the nucleus of cells and are not specific for dermatomyositis.

question:
A 37-year-old female presents with pain and stiffness in her hands. Her symptoms are worse in the morning and seem to improve throughout the day. She has recently returned from a holiday in Ibiza and is taking the oral contraceptive pill. On examination, she has bilateral swelling and tenderness in the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Inflammatory arthritis involving DIP swelling and dactylitis points to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis

Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. It can involve any joint in the body, but unlike rheumatoid arthritis often affects the distal interphalangeal joints. Other common symptoms of psoriatic arthritis include dactylitis 'sausage digit', inflammation of an entire digit and nail changes such as onycholysis. In 15-20% of cases, symptoms of arthritis are detected before psoriasis appears.

Gonococcal arthritis is a single or multiple joint septic arthritis caused by disseminated gonococcal infection.

Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome), is an inflammatory arthritis that develops in response to an infection. The classic triad of symptoms is inflammatory arthritis of large joints, inflammation of the eyes (conjunctivitis or uveitis), and urethritis/cervicitis.

Reactive arthritis: conjunctivitis/uveitis, urethritis/cervicitis and arthritis 'can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'

Rheumatoid arthritis classicly presents as a symmetrical polyarthritis, but typically it does not involve the distal interphalangeal joints.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that has a wide range of clinical and laboratory features which can be remembered using the pneumonic 'SOAP BRAIN MD'.

'SOAP BRAIN MD'

Serositis: pleurisy or pericarditis
Oral ulcers
Arthritis
Photosensitivity

Blood: anaemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia
Renal disorder: lupus nephritis - minimal mesangial, mesangial proliferative, focal, diffuse, membranous and advanced sclerosis
Antinuclear antibody
Immunology: anti-Smith, anti-ds DNA and antiphospholipid antibody
Neurologic disorder: seizures or psychosis

Malar rash
Discoid rash

question: A 28-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis asks for advice about conception. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Methotrexate may be continued during pregnancy as long as the woman takes folic acid 5mg daily
NSAIDs should be avoided in the first and second trimester
Woman with rheumatoid should be encouraged to conceive as soon as possible (ideally within 1 year) after diagnosis to minimise the risk of complications
TNF-α blockers are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy
Hydroxychloroquine is considered safe during pregnancy
correctText: Hydroxychloroquine is considered safe during pregnancy

question: A 65-year-old woman attends the rheumatology clinic following a low-impact wrist fracture. A DEXA scan is performed, and her T score at the femoral neck is -2.6. She asks what this value means. Which statement best explains the basis of the T score measurement?
options: It compares her bone mass to that of young adults
It adjusts for age, gender, and ethnicity
It reflects risk of future fractures only
It measures bone turnover markers directly
It compares her bone mass to people of similar age
correctText: It compares her bone mass to that of young adults
explanation:
DEXA scans: the T score is based on bone mass of young reference population

It compares her bone mass to that of young adults

: This is correct. The T score from a DEXA scan represents how many standard deviations a patient’s bone mineral density (BMD) is above or below the mean BMD of a healthy young adult reference population (typically aged 20–30). This approach allows clinicians to quantify osteoporosis risk based on how much a patient's bones have deviated from peak bone mass, which occurs in youth. In UK clinical practice, this underpins both diagnosis and management decisions: a T score ≤-2.5 defines osteoporosis according to WHO criteria.

It adjusts for age, gender, and ethnicity

: This describes the Z score rather than the T score. The Z score assesses BMD relative to an age-matched population with similar demographic characteristics but does not form the basis for diagnosing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women or men over 50.

It reflects risk of future fractures only

: While lower T scores are associated with increased fracture risk, the T score itself is specifically a statistical comparison to young adult mean BMD; it does not directly measure fracture risk alone but provides information used alongside other factors in risk assessment tools such as FRAX.

It measures bone turnover markers directly

: Bone turnover markers are biochemical tests (e.g., serum CTX or P1NP), not imaging-based indices like the DEXA-derived T score. The T score is purely based on radiological assessment.

It compares her bone mass to people of similar age

: This again refers to the Z score rather than the T score. For diagnostic purposes in older adults, clinicians rely on how far BMD has fallen compared with youthful peak values—not peers—because this better predicts fragility.

question:
A 42-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of shoulder pain. The pain is localised to the left shoulder with no radiation.

She recalls hurting her shoulder following attempting shoulder exercises in the gym recently.

She has a past medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypercholesterolemia.

On examination, the shoulder feels normal temperature and colour. It does not appear swollen. External rotation is significantly limited by pain on both active and passive movements. Flexion, extension, abduction and adduction are also limited by pain, but less so.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
External rotation (on both active and passive movement) is classically impaired in adhesive capsulitis

Adhesive capsulitis

is correct. Adhesive capsulitis is more commonly seen in middle-aged females, diabetic patients and following trauma. External rotation is usually the most affected movement.

Calcific tendonosis

is incorrect. This would present with bursitis: with pain and restriction in movement, and the shoulder would feel hot and swollen.

Cervical nerve root entrapment

is incorrect. This would present with pain in the neck and/or shoulder. The patient would be likely to describe the pain radiating to the arm, or describe numbness/paraesthesia. Neck range of movement would likely be impaired.

Supraspinatus tendonosis and torn rotator cuff

are incorrect. In these cases, the most prominent restriction in movement would be impaired abduction.

question: You are doing the annual review of a 50-year-old woman who has rheumatoid arthritis. Which one of the following complications is most likely to occur as a result of her disease?
explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis: patients have an increased risk of IHD

The correct answer is

Ischaemic heart disease

. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic inflammatory disease that primarily affects the joints. However, it also has several extra-articular manifestations and comorbidities. One of the most significant of these is cardiovascular disease, particularly ischaemic heart disease. This increased risk is due to both the systemic inflammation associated with RA and the higher prevalence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors in individuals with RA.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia

is not typically associated with rheumatoid arthritis. While there may be an overall slightly increased risk of haematological malignancies in patients with RA, this association appears to be stronger for lymphomas rather than leukaemias.

Hypertension

can occur in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, but it's not directly caused by the disease itself. It's more likely to be related to other factors such as age, lifestyle or use of certain medications like non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which are commonly used in RA treatment.

Colorectal cancer

also does not have a direct relationship with rheumatoid arthritis. There may be an increased risk due to chronic inflammation or immunosuppressive therapy but this link isn't as strong as that between RA and cardiovascular diseases.

Finally,

Type 2 diabetes mellitus

has been found to have a bidirectional relationship with rheumatoid arthritis - people with RA have a higher risk of developing Type 2 diabetes, and people with Type 2 diabetes have a higher risk of developing RA. However, the likelihood of developing ischemic heart disease remains higher in patients with rheumatoid arthritis compared to type 2 diabetes mellitus.

question:
A 45-year-old is referred to the clinic due to recurrent, progressive episodes of illness, affecting different sites of her body. She reports that the episodes can result in pain in several areas including the nose, eyes, ears and joints. No clear diagnosis has been established despite several specialists' input.

She currently feels her symptoms are 'flaring' and describes pain around the ears, nose, large joint with associated breathlessness and a mild cough. On exam, there is redness and swelling of the ears and a collapse of the nasal bridge. A mild wheeze is heard on the chest.

On review of her notes, she has had previous episodes of scleritis/iritis and is under investigation for hearing loss.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
As well as ear problems, relapsing polychondritis may present with nasal chondritis, respiratory tract involvement and arthralgia

This patient has presented with features most in keeping with the autoimmune condition of relapsing polychondritis. This is a multi-system condition associated with repeat episodes of cartilage inflammation and deterioration. Common examples of areas affected, and therefore symptoms patients present with, include the ears (auricular chondritis, vertigo, hearing loss), the nose (saddle nose deformity), the respiratory tract (wheezing, inspiratory stridor, voice changes), the eyes (episcleritis, scleritis, iritis,) and the joints (arthralgia). Although there are several conditions that present with similar features, the involvement of the ears and nose in a multi-system disease is characteristic of relapsing polychondritis. Given its multi-organ involvement, various scoring systems have been created, based on clinical, pathological, and radiological criteria, to assist make the diagnosis.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) is a differential however it is not the most likely diagnosis as this condition generally only affects the basement membranes of the kidneys and the lungs. Patients with this condition normally present with symptoms of haemoptysis, chest discomfort, shortness of breath and features of renal impairment. Several features of this case, including the ear, nasal, joint and ocular involvement are not associated with Goodpasture syndrome.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome) is a similar autoimmune condition that causes inflammation of the small and medium-sized blood vessels, commonly in patients with a history of airway allergic hypersensitivity. The disease normally is made up of 3 phases including an early prodromal stage (patients experience allergic rhinitis and asthma symptom), a hypereosinophilia stage mainly affecting the lungs and gastrointestinal (GI) tract (patient may experience weight loss, night sweats, abdominal pain and GI bleeding) and finally a full vasculitic stage (resulting in reduced blood flow to the organs, ischaemia and widespread cell death). It would be very unusual for a patient to present in this final vasculitic stage. Also, as it is only the blood vessels that are affected there are again features seen in this case that would not be explained by the syndrome including the saddle-nose deformity, ocular, ear or joint involvement.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a condition that involves the formation of granulomas and vasculitis. The features of saddle-nose deformity and ocular involvement can be seen in GPA however as it affects the blood vessels, involvement of the ears/hearing is not associated with the condition.

Reactive arthritis is a form of inflammatory arthritis triggered by a preceding infection, normally genitourinary (e.g.

Chlamydia

) or gastrointestinal (e.g.

Salmonella

or

Campylobacter

) in nature. Patients classically present with the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and urethritis or cervicitis. Again nasal deformity and ear involvement are not seen in reactive arthritis.

question:
A 45-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology clinic for review. She reports a six-month history of arthralgia and swelling affecting the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of both hands.

On examination, she has boggy swelling of the third, fourth and fifth MCP joints bilaterally, with erythema and mild tenderness to palpation. No gross deformities are noted in either hand, and she has a normal range of motion and motor function bilaterally.

Investigation results are shown below:


Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibody titre	48U	(<20)

What is the most likely hand X-ray findings for this patient?
explanation:
Juxta-articular osteoporosis/osteopenia is an early x-ray feature of rheumatoid arthritis

The correct answer is

juxta-articular osteopaenia

. This patient has a likely new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. This is based on the symmetrical arthropathy affecting multiple joints in her hands, with a positive anti-CCP titre. Juxta-articular osteopenia is a common early X-ray feature of rheumatoid arthritis and is the most likely finding in this clinical scenario.

Joint subluxation

is incorrect. Although this can be seen in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, it would be unlikely to be present on an initial X-ray at the point of diagnosis, and usually occurs in the context of progressive disease. In addition, the clinical examination findings do not suggest the presence of joint subluxation.

Peri-articular erosions

is incorrect. These would also be seen in the context of progressive rheumatoid arthritis, and are not classically seen on initial diagnostic X-rays.

Subchondral cysts

is incorrect. These tend to be seen on the X-rays of patients with osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis.

Subchondral sclerosis

is incorrect. These are also X-ray findings suggestive of osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis.

question:
A 40-year-old woman presents to the clinic with pain on the radial side of her right wrist. She reports difficulty gripping objects and mentions that her pain worsens when lifting her infant.

On examination, there is tenderness over the radial styloid process, and she experiences pain when moving her thumb, particularly when abducting the thumb against resistance.

An X-ray demonstrates soft-tissue swelling over the radial styloid only.

Which clinical test would be most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Pain on the radial side of the wrist/tenderness over the radial styloid process ? De Quervain's tenosynovitis

Finkelstein test

is the correct answer. The most likely diagnosis in this scenario is de Quervain’s tenosynovitis, based on the patient’s symptoms and subtle X-ray findings. The patient reports pain on the radial aspect of the wrist, difficulty gripping, and tenderness at the radial styloid process—hallmark features of de Quervain’s tenosynovitis. While primarily a clinical diagnosis, X-rays may show soft tissue swelling or help exclude alternative conditions. This condition involves inflammation of the sheath surrounding the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus tendons, causing pain and impaired thumb function. The Finkelstein test is a key diagnostic manoeuvre, performed by grasping the patient’s thumb and ulnar deviating the wrist. Sharp pain along the distal radius confirms the diagnosis, reflecting inflammation of the tendon sheaths.

Allen’s test

evaluates radial and ulnar artery patency, typically preceding arterial blood sampling or surgical interventions, by assessing hand perfusion. Given that our patient presents with symptoms indicative of tendinous rather than vascular pathology—namely, pain localised to the radial aspect of the wrist accompanied by difficulty in thumb movements—Allen's test does not pertain to this clinical picture.

Phalen’s test

assists in diagnosing carpal tunnel syndrome by reproducing median nerve compression symptoms when maintaining wrist flexion for a prolonged duration. However, our patient's complaints—radial-sided wrist pain accentuated over the radial styloid process coupled with impaired thumb activity—are characteristic of de Quervain's tenosynovitis rather than median nerve entrapment.

Mill's test

is primarily used to diagnose lateral epicondylitis, or tennis elbow, which presents as pain over the lateral epicondyle of the elbow rather than at the wrist. In this case, symptoms such as tenderness over the radial styloid process and pain with thumb movements are more indicative of a condition involving the wrist and thumb, specifically de Quervain's tenosynovitis. Mill's test is not designed to identify this condition, as it targets a different anatomical region and pathology.

Spurling’s test

is designed to evaluate cervical radiculopathy resulting from nerve root compression within the cervical spine. During this examination, head tilting towards the affected side combined with applied downward pressure may reproduce radicular arm sensations if positive for nerve root irritation. In this case, wrist pain on the radial side plus sensitivity overlying the radial styloid are indicative of tendon-related inflammation seen in de Quervain's tenosynovitis rather than cervical nerve impingement; thus Spurling’s test lacks relevance here.

question: A 28-year-old woman who has rheumatoid arthritis is to be started on etanercept injections after failing to respond to methotrexate and sulfsalazine. Which one of the following adverse effects is associated with the use of etanercept?
explanation:
T

The correct answer is

Reactivation of tuberculosis

. Etanercept, a tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor, can lead to reactivation of latent tuberculosis (TB). This is because TNF plays a crucial role in granuloma formation and containment of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Therefore, inhibiting TNF can disrupt these granulomas and allow for reactivation of the disease. In the UK, guidelines recommend screening for latent TB before starting treatment with etanercept or other TNF inhibitors.

Triggering Churg-Strauss syndrome

is not associated with etanercept use. Churg-Strauss syndrome, also known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), is an autoimmune condition that causes inflammation and damage to blood vessels. It's typically associated with asthma and high levels of eosinophils - a type of white blood cell. There's no evidence to suggest that etanercept triggers this syndrome.

Thrombocytosis

, an abnormally high platelet count, is not a recognised side effect of etanercept. Thrombocytosis can occur due to various conditions such as infection, inflammation, cancer or certain blood disorders but it's not linked directly to etanercept use.

Regarding

Tendonitis

, while rheumatoid arthritis itself can cause tendinitis due to chronic inflammation, there's no clear evidence suggesting that etanercept increases the risk of developing tendonitis.

Lastly,

Cardiomyopathy

, a disease of the heart muscle that makes it harder for your heart to pump blood to the rest of your body, is also not directly related to etanercept use. While rheumatoid arthritis patients have an increased risk for cardiovascular diseases due to systemic inflammation and other factors, this isn't specifically linked to the use of etanercept.

question: Which of the following is least likely to be associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis features - the 'A's

The correct answer is

Achalasia

. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the axial skeleton, particularly the sacroiliac joints and spine. It can also present with extra-articular manifestations, but Achalasia is not typically associated with AS. Achalasia is a disorder of the oesophagus where it loses its ability to move food along, resulting in difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, and sometimes chest pain. The cause of achalasia is unknown and it's generally not linked with inflammatory conditions like AS.

Apical fibrosis

can be seen in patients with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis. This condition causes fibrotic changes at the apices of the lungs due to chronic inflammation. Although this manifestation is rare, it has been documented in the literature.

Achilles tendonitis

is another common manifestation in ankylosing spondylitis. Enthesitis or inflammation of sites where tendons or ligaments insert into bone can occur in up to 50% of patients with AS. The Achilles tendon is one of the most commonly affected sites.

Amyloidosis

, specifically secondary amyloidosis (AA), can occur as a complication of chronic inflammatory diseases including ankylosing spondylitis if there's persistent high disease activity over many years without appropriate treatment control.

Finally,

Heart block

can also be associated with ankylosing spondylitis. Cardiovascular complications are well recognized in AS and include aortitis, aortic regurgitation, and conduction disturbances such as heart block which may require pacemaker insertion if severe.

question:
An 81-year-old man attends the emergency department with acute knee pain. He has no other symptoms. Observations and investigations are as follows.


Respiratory rate 18/min
Oxygen saturations 99% on air
Heart rate 72/min
Blood pressure 140/71mmHg
Temperature 36.6ºC


Hb	144 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	390 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	16.4 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
CRP	42 mg/L	(< 5)


X-ray right knee	Normal joint space. Prominent calcification of the menisci and articular cartilage
Synovial fluid microscopy and culture	White blood cells: 1700/mm³. No growth at 48 hours

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chondrocalcinosis helps to distinguish pseudogout from gout

The correct answer is

pseudogout

. Also known as calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, this is a crystal arthropathy that presents similarly to gout. Lack of crystals on microscopy would not rule these out as the sensitivity is less than 100%. The key clue here is chondrocalcinosis, the finding of calcification of the articular cartilage. Although not specific, this is suggestive of pseudogout. In the knee, this often manifests as calcification of the menisci.

Gout

is incorrect. Clinically this is hard to distinguish from pseudogout. As discussed above, the x-ray findings are more suggestive of pseudogout here.

Osteoarthritis

is incorrect. This typically presents with chronic rather than acute joint pain. X-ray features include narrowing of the joint space, formation of osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis and cysts. White blood cells would also not be expected in the synovial fluid in osteoarthritis.

Reactive arthritis

is incorrect. This most commonly affects younger patients and generally occurs after an infective trigger such as a sexually-transmitted infection or a diarrhoeal illness. The joint pain is often accompanied by conjunctivitis and urethritis, which are not present here. It also would not explain the x-ray findings.

Septic arthritis

is incorrect. This refers to bacterial infection of the joint which usually occurs by haematogenous spread. The joint is generally extremely painful with minimal range of movement and patients are often unwell with systemic upset, which is not the case here. In the absence of recent antibiotics, culture at 48 hours is very sensitive as the most common organisms (such as

Staphylococcus aureus

and

Streptococcus pyogenes

) are fairly easy to culture.

question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the GP with a several-month history of troublesome symptoms. She describes generalised weakness of her arms and legs, as well as a rash over her back and shoulders. She also describes a rash around her eyes and roughened, red patches over her fingers.

On examination, she has a macular rash over the back and shoulders, a heliotrope rash periorbitally and roughened red papules over the extensor surfaces of the fingers. Examination of the limbs demonstrates proximal weakness.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following antibodies is most specific?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis antibodies: ANA most common, anti-Mi-2 most specific

The diagnosis here is that of dermatomyositis, given the proximal muscle weakness and classic dermatological findings. Raynaud's phenomenon may also be present, as it is here. The correct answer is anti-Mi-2 antibodies, as these are most specific for the condition.

Anti-ribonuclear protein antibodies are incorrect - these would be present in mixed connective tissue disease. This is a difficult diagnosis to make and would have more symptoms than seen in this scenario, including symptoms from multiple, overlapping conditions. Features of CREST syndrome may be seen, as well as systemic lupus erythematosus, in addition to those seen here.

Anti-centromere antibodies are incorrect - these are found in CREST syndrome, which would present differently to this scenario - calcinosis, Raynaud's, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia.

Antinuclear antibodies are incorrect - these are the most common antibody type found in dermatomyositis, but not the most specific. Indeed, they are found in many rheumatological conditions.

Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are incorrect - this would be more specific for polymyositis. This overlaps with the presentation of dermatomyositis, but with more prominence on the muscular features rather than the dermatological features.

question:
A 40-year-old woman is reviewed in the rheumatology clinic. She describes a 3-month history of progressive pain, swelling and stiffness in the joints of both her hands, particularly her wrists. Her blood test results are summarised below. The doctor reviews her hand X-rays.


ANA	Positive
Anti-CCP	Positive
Rheumatoid Factor	Negative

Given the likely diagnosis, what is an early X-ray feature of the disease?
explanation:
Juxta-articular osteoporosis/osteopenia is an early x-ray feature of rheumatoid arthritis

The disease being described is rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Patients often complain of symmetrical polyarticular inflammatory arthritis, most commonly affecting the metacarpophalangeal joints. The positive anti-CCP test is both sensitive and specific for RA.

Early X-ray changes in RA include loss of joint space and

juxta-articular osteopaenia

.

Later in poorly-controlled RA, X-ray findings might include

articular erosions

and

subluxation

. These findings are increasingly uncommon with the increased access to disease-modifying medications such as methotrexate.

Subarticular sclerosis

and

subchondral cysts

are findings on X-ray associated with osteoarthritis (OA) rather than RA, so they are incorrect. OA more typically affects weight-bearing joints such as hips and knees. It may cause pain and swelling but not true stiffness. OA would not account for the positive autoantibody screen results.

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with a four week history of shoulder pain. There has been no obvious precipitating injury and no previous experience. The pain is worse on movement and there is a grating sensation if she moves the arm too quickly. She also gets pain at night, particularly when she lies on the affected shoulder. On examination there is no obvious erythema or swelling. Passive abduction is painful between between 60 and 120 degrees. She is unable to abduct the arm herself past 70-80 degrees. Flexion and extension are preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 18-year-old boy presented with sudden onset acute pain in the right hip for 9-days. The pain, associated with high-grade fever with chills, was non-radiating, severe in intensity and aggravated by movements at the hip, and was only partly relieved with analgesia. The fever was remittent and was relieved with paracetamol but only to reoccur. He denies any history of trauma.

What is the key investigation in this case given the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Synovial fluid sampling is the key investigation in patients with suspected septic arthritis

Septic arthritis is an inflammatory joint condition secondary to joint inoculation with infectious microorganisms.

Synovial fluid analysis

is the key investigation in patients with suspected septic arthritis that includes culture and is the cornerstone of diagnosis and should be performed prior to antibiotic therapy being administered. It enables the diagnoses of both sepsis and crystal-induced arthritis to be confirmed quickly and therefore is the correct answer.

Right hip x-ray

is unlikely to be useful in the acute stage of septic arthritis as it is likely to remain normal. It may show a narrowing of the joint space due to cartilage destruction or joint effusion. Therefore it is considered a key investigation.

CT right hip

similarly shows features found on radiographs however a fat-fluid level can be a specific sign in the absence of trauma.

Bone scans

perform well for distinguishing sepsis from osteoarthrosis, but cannot distinguish effectively between sepsis and other causes of joint inflammation making its value limited in this case.

Blood cultures

may help to identify the causative organism in cases where synovial fluid culture remains unrewarding. Whilst taking blood cultures is a necessary part of the septic screen, synovial fluid analysis remains fundamental.

question: A 48- year-old patient presented to her family physician complaining of pain all over her body for the past 4 months. She initially thought it was because she started taking aerobic exercise classes 6 months ago. However, the pain has been persistently bothering her and taking over-the-counter pain relievers did not help. The pain is more pronounced around her shoulders and lower back. She also complains feeling tired and not being able to sleep because of the pain. She has a body mass index of 28 kg per m2 and has never smoked in her life. She denies any weight loss or episodes of fever. She currently lives alone and is usually able to do her household chores. Her mother who passed away last year suffered from rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, the doctor finds that the patient has tender areas on her neck, elbow regions, and knees. Which is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

A 25-year-old presents with repeated episodes of severe muscle cramping and dark-coloured urine following short bouts of intense exercise. He reports that his symptoms improve with rest but recur with similar exertion.

There is no significant family history, and he denies the use of steroids or other performance-enhancing drugs.

Blood and urine:


Hb	138 g/L	(135-175)
WCC	6.5 x10⁹/L	(4.0-11.0)
Plat	240 x10⁹/L	(150-450)
CK	25,000 U/L	(< 200)
Myoglobin (serum)	1,000 µg/L	(< 70)
Urea	7.5 mmol/L	(2.5-7.8)
Cr	110 µmol/L	(60-110)
Urine myoglobin	Positive	Negative
Urine dipstick	Blood 3+	Negative

What is the mechanism of the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Repeated cramping, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria after short bouts of exercise  can point towards McArdle's disease

This patient’s history of repeated cramping, rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobinuria after short bouts of exercise strongly suggests McArdle's disease, a glycogen storage disorder. The presentation, including marked elevations in CK and serum myoglobin, aligns with impaired energy metabolism in skeletal muscle. McArdle's disease is caused by

myophosphorylase deficiency

, an enzyme critical for glycogen breakdown in muscle cells. Without functional myophosphorylase, muscles cannot effectively utilise glycogen as a rapid energy source during exertion, leading to muscle breakdown and the characteristic symptoms. The disorder's hallmark is exercise intolerance during short, intense activity, as seen in this case. The presence of urine myoglobin further indicates muscle injury. Recognising these symptoms and the associated enzymatic deficiency is essential for diagnosing McArdle’s disease and differentiating it from other metabolic myopathies.

Acid maltase deficiency

is incorrect because it leads to glycogen accumulation in lysosomes, causing Pompe disease. This condition typically presents with progressive muscle weakness, respiratory insufficiency, and cardiomyopathy rather than acute exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis. Symptoms do not resolve with rest and are unrelated to short-term glycogen mobilisation failures, as seen in McArdle’s disease.

Aldolase A deficiency

is incorrect because this glycolytic enzyme deficiency impairs energy production in both skeletal muscle and erythrocytes. While patients may experience muscle cramps during exercise, they also present with chronic haemolytic anaemia, a finding absent in this case. Additionally, Aldolase A deficiency is not associated with the classic features of rhabdomyolysis or myoglobinuria following short, intense exercise bouts.

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency

is incorrect as it is a disorder of fatty acid oxidation. Symptoms occur after prolonged fasting or sustained exercise when fat metabolism becomes the primary energy source. Unlike McArdle’s disease, episodes are triggered by long-term energy demands, not short, high-intensity efforts, and rhabdomyolysis is associated with prolonged exercise or metabolic stress.

Phosphofructokinase deficiency

is incorrect as it causes Tarui disease, another glycolytic pathway disorder. It results in muscle pain, fatigue, and exercise intolerance during sustained, submaximal activity. Haemolysis is also a feature due to red blood cell involvement. The clinical pattern differs from McArdle’s disease, which is triggered by brief, high-intensity exercise and does not involve haemolytic anaemia.

question: A 62-year-old man with lung cancer is suspected of having dermatomyositis. Which one of the following antibodies is most likely to be positive?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis antibodies: ANA most common, anti-Mi-2 most specific

In dermatomyositis associated with lung cancer,

anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA)

are most likely to be positive. ANA is a sensitive but non-specific marker found in many autoimmune conditions, including dermatomyositis. In cancer-associated dermatomyositis, ANA positivity is particularly common, making it a useful screening test when malignancy is suspected in conjunction with dermatomyositis symptoms.

Anti-centromere bodies

are typically associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (formerly known as CREST syndrome) rather than dermatomyositis. These antibodies are highly specific for systemic sclerosis and are not characteristically elevated in cancer-associated dermatomyositis.

Anti-scl-70 antibodies

(also known as anti-topoisomerase I antibodies) are primarily associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. They are not typically elevated in dermatomyositis and would not be the most useful diagnostic marker in this clinical scenario.

Anti-Jo-1 antibodies

are associated with antisynthetase syndrome, a subset of inflammatory myopathies. While they can be present in dermatomyositis, they are more commonly associated with interstitial lung disease rather than malignancy-associated dermatomyositis.

Anti-Mi-2 antibodies

are indeed associated with dermatomyositis, but they are typically found in classic dermatomyositis without associated malignancy. In fact, the presence of anti-Mi-2 antibodies generally indicates a better prognosis and lower risk of associated malignancy.

question:
A 79-year-old man presents with a history of lower back pain and right hip pain. Blood tests reveal the following:


Calcium	2.20 mmol/l
Phosphate	0.8 mmol/l
ALP	890 u/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Paget's disease - old man, bone pain, raised ALP

The normal calcium and phosphate combined with a raised alkaline phosphate points to a diagnosis of Paget's

question:
A 29-year-old man visits his general practitioner with a 1-week history of left knee pain. He complains of pain on weight-bearing and swelling around the joint. There is no pain in his other joints although he does complain of pain when passing urine.

On examination, he has a temperature of 37.9ºC. His left knee is swollen and slightly warm to the touch. He has inflamed conjunctivae.


Hb	151 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	333 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	7.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
CRP	99 mg/L	(< 5)

A knee joint aspiration is taken.

What would be expected to be found on the joint aspirate?
options: No organism growth on gram stain
correctText: No organism growth on gram stain
explanation:
Reactive arthritis: develops after an infection where the organism cannot be recovered from the joint

No organism growth on gram stain

is correct. This patient has reactive arthritis a HLA-B27 associated seronegative spondyloarthropathy. Classically, the triad of symptoms: arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis will be seen. Reactive arthritis commonly occurs following a diarrhoeal illness or sexually transmitted disease (e.g.

Chlamydia trachomatis

). Given the dysuria, it seems that a sexually transmitted disease may be the trigger for reactive arthritis. Unlike other causes of infective arthritis (e.g. septic arthritis and disseminated gonococcal arthritis) in reactive arthritis, an organism cannot be recovered from the affected joint.

Gram negative cocci

is incorrect. These may be seen secondary to infection with

Neisseria gonorrhoeae

. It is a common cause of septic arthritis in young adults due to haematogenous spread of the infection. Additional symptoms include tenosynovitis, migratory polyarthritis and dermatitis. Although this patient has dysuria that is suggestive of a sexually-transmitted disease, the absence of these symptoms in the patient makes reactive arthritis more likely.

Gram positive cocci

is incorrect. This would likely be positive in a patient with septic arthritis that is characterised by an acutely inflamed isolated joint. The joint is typically erythematous and swollen associated with a fever and restricted movement. Common organisms include

Staphylococcus aureus

. There are some similarities seen in this patient. However, given the presence of dysuria and conjunctivitis, reactive arthritis is more likely.

Negative birefringent crystals

is incorrect. This is typically seen in cases of gout which is characterised by an acutely inflamed joint (most commonly the 1st metatarsal). Gout is usually seen in men (typically over 40 years) and is associated with a diet high in meat content.

Positive birefringent crystals

is incorrect. This is associated with pseudogout which is caused by the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate. It is more common in the elderly and is often precipitated by dehydration or intercurrent illness. It does not explain this patient's symptoms.

question: A 40-year-old woman complains of a permanent 'funny-bone' sensation in her right elbow. This is accompanied by tingling in the little and ring finger. Her symptoms are worse when the elbow is bent for prolonged periods. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 50-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid presents with a suspected septic knee joint. A diagnostic aspiration is performed and sent to microbiology. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Septic arthritis - most common organism:

The correct answer is

Staphylococcus aureus

. This organism is the most common cause of septic arthritis in adults. It can enter the bloodstream from a distant site and then infect the joint, or it can be introduced directly into the joint during trauma or surgery. In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, damage to the joint lining can also increase susceptibility to infection.

Staphylococcus epidermidis

is less likely to be responsible for septic arthritis in this patient. While it is a common skin commensal and can cause infection following prosthetic joint surgery, it's not typically associated with septic arthritis in native joints.

Escherichia coli

, while a common cause of urinary tract infections and abdominal sepsis, is not often found as a causative agent in septic arthritis. However, in patients with risk factors such as diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression, Gram-negative organisms like E.coli may indeed be implicated.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae

could potentially cause a septic knee joint but this is more likely in sexually active younger individuals rather than a 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis. Gonococcal arthritis often presents differently too, typically as part of a syndrome that includes tenosynovitis, dermatitis and migratory polyarthralgia.

Finally,

Streptococcus pneumoniae

is an unlikely culprit for this patient's condition. While S.pneumoniae does occasionally cause joint infections, these are rare and usually occur after bacteremia from pneumococcal pneumonia or meningitis. It's much less commonly seen as a cause of septic arthritis compared to Staphylococcus aureus.

question: What is the minimum steroid intake a patient should be taking before they are offered osteoporosis prophylaxis?
options: Equivalent of prednisolone 10 mg or more each day for 6 months
Equivalent of prednisolone 7.5 mg or more each day for 6 weeks
Equivalent of prednisolone 5 mg or more each day for 6 weeks
Equivalent of prednisolone 7.5 mg or more each day for 3 months
Equivalent of prednisolone 10 mg or more each day for 6 weeks
correctText: Equivalent of prednisolone 7.5 mg or more each day for 3 months

question:
A 22-year-old gymnast reports pain in the lateral forearm that is worse on straightening the wrist or fingers. She also sometimes feels an unusual sensation in her hand a bit like pins and needles. On examination, she is tender distal to the common extensor origin with no pain overlying the lateral epicondyle itself.

What is the most likely cause of her forearm pain?
explanation:
Radial tunnel syndrome presents similarly to lateral epicondylitis however pain is typically distal to the epicondyle and worse on elbow extension/forearm pronation

Radial tunnel syndrome can be difficult to distinguish from lateral epicondylitis as both conditions present with lateral elbow pain. Radial tunnel syndrome however typically presents with tenderness distal to the common extensor origin in comparison to lateral epicondylitis where there is pain over the common extensor origin.  It is most common in gymnasts, racquet players and golfers who frequently hyperextend at the wrist or carry out frequent supination/pronation.  Patients can also complain of hand paraesthesia or aching at the wrist.

Cubital tunnel syndrome patients experience tingling and numbness in the 4th and 5th finger.

In olecranon bursitis, there would be presence of swelling over the posterior elbow.

Cervical radiculopathy would cause a burning pain radiating from shoulder to fingers. There may be reduced cervical range of motion or pain as clues in the history.

question:
A 36-year-old woman presents with progressive tingling and numbness of the 4th and 5th fingers of her right hand. Initially, this was intermittent but recently has become constant. She notices that the symptoms are worse when leaning on her right elbow. She recalls hitting her elbow against a door some time ago.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cubital tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the ulnar nerve and can present with tingling/numbness of the 4th and 5th finger

The correct answer is cubital tunnel syndrome. The ulnar nerve runs through the cubital tunnel and compression of this will lead to the symptoms described - tingling and numbness of the 4th and 5th fingers. Management is often conservative but surgery may be required.

Carpal tunnel syndrome is due to compression of the median nerve at the wrist, where it runs through the carpal tunnel. This would present with generalised pain and tingling of the hand and wrist, not specifically the 4th and 5th fingers.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis would present differently, with pain on movement of the thumb/wrist. The radial styloid may be hardened and thickened.

Medial epicondylitis, or golfer's elbow, would present with pain along the medial elbow, close to the cubital tunnel - but localised to the area as it is a tendinopathy, and not compression of the nerve.

Radial tunnel syndrome, as the name suggests, is due to compression of the radial nerve and may lead to tingling/numbness/pain along the back of the hand and forearm.

question:
A 19-year-old man presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, most noticeable after exertion such as playing football. He has fixed weakness in his upper legs and arms, difficulty climbing stairs, occasional muscle pain and stiffness, and cola-coloured urine post-exercise. Graded exercise testing shows a 'second-wind phenomenon'—improved tolerance after brief rest. His blood investigations reveal:


Creatine Kinase (CK)	1,500 IU/L	(40 - 300)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Repeated cramping, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria after short bouts of exercise  can point towards McArdle's disease

McArdle’s disease

is the correct answer. McArdle’s disease is a glycogen storage disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme muscle phosphorylase, which is needed for glycogen breakdown during exercise. This results in exercise intolerance with muscle pain, stiffness, and fixed proximal weakness, particularly after exertion. The patient's report of cola-coloured urine suggests myoglobinuria, which reflects muscle breakdown. The second-wind phenomenon, where symptoms improve after a short rest, remains a characteristic clinical clue and indicates a shift from anaerobic to aerobic metabolism. The elevated CK supports muscle injury related to exertion.

Becker muscular dystrophy

is a slowly progressive X-linked muscular dystrophy that commonly presents in adolescence with proximal muscle weakness, especially in the pelvic and thigh muscles. While elevated CK levels and muscle wasting may be seen, the presentation is usually more chronic and insidious, and it does not typically involve exercise-induced myoglobinuria. The second-wind phenomenon is not characteristic of this disorder, and weakness tends to be more constant rather than triggered or worsened by physical activity. The acute symptom onset after exercise, as seen in this patient, makes McArdle’s disease a more appropriate diagnosis.

Mitochondrial myopathies

can cause exercise intolerance, proximal muscle weakness, and elevated CK, which might make them a potential consideration. However, they are usually associated with multisystem involvement, such as ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, hearing loss, or cardiomyopathy, none of which are noted in this case. Additionally, myoglobinuria is not a common feature, and the second-wind phenomenon is not typically observed. The absence of systemic findings and the presence of exertion-induced symptoms with recovery after rest favour McArdle’s disease over a mitochondrial disorder.

Polymyalgia rheumatica

is highly unlikely in this case due to the patient’s age—it almost exclusively affects individuals over the age of 50. It presents with bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, rather than true muscle weakness or wasting. Myoglobinuria is not a feature, and CK levels are usually normal or only mildly elevated. The presence of exercise-induced symptoms, second-wind phenomenon, and myoglobinuria argue strongly against this diagnosis. These findings suggest a metabolic myopathy rather than an inflammatory rheumatological condition.

Polymyositis

is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy that causes gradual-onset proximal muscle weakness and elevated CK levels, often with systemic features such as fatigue and weight loss. However, it is rare in adolescents, and the pattern of exercise-related worsening and myoglobinuria seen in this patient is not typical. Second-wind phenomenon is not observed in polymyositis, and the improvement of symptoms with rest points away from a chronic inflammatory process. Muscle wasting can occur, but not in the acute-onset, exertion-linked pattern described here.

question:
A 25-year-old woman is referred to a genetics clinic due to concerns about hypermobility and easy bruising. She reports a long history of joint pain and frequent joint dislocations with minimal trauma. Her skin appears unusually stretchy, and she has multiple small scars on her knees and elbows from minor injuries. She confirms a family history of similar symptoms, including a cousin who experienced a spontaneous arterial rupture.

Examination reveals hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, and multiple atrophic scars.

What is the most common defect associated with this patient’s condition?
explanation:
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is most commonly associated with a defect in type III collagen

This patient most likely has Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), a group of connective tissue disorders primarily caused by defects in collagen synthesis or structure. The features of hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, atrophic scars, and a family history of vascular complications align with the clinical presentation of EDS, particularly the vascular subtype.

Type III collagen

is the most commonly implicated defect in EDS, especially in the vascular subtype, leading to weakened blood vessels and other connective tissues. This explains the patient's easy bruising, hypermobility, and the family history of arterial rupture, hallmark features of a defect in type III collagen.

Elastin

is a key component of elastic fibres in the skin, lungs, and blood vessels. Defects in elastin are linked to Williams syndrome, characterised by distinctive facial features, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and developmental delays. This patient's symptoms of joint hypermobility, skin changes, and vascular fragility are consistent with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome which is not due to a defect in elastin.

Fibrillin-1

is a glycoprotein crucial for the formation of elastic fibres. Mutations in fibrillin-1 cause Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder characterised by tall stature, long limbs, lens dislocation, and aortic aneurysms. Unlike Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome does not typically feature hyperextensible skin or atrophic scars. This patient’s presentation aligns more with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, making fibrillin-1 defects unlikely.

Type I collagen

is the primary collagen in bones, skin, and tendons. Defects in type I collagen are associated with osteogenesis imperfecta, which presents with brittle bones, recurrent fractures, and blue sclerae. These features differ significantly from the hypermobility, skin extensibility, and vascular complications seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Since this patient's presentation lacks bone fragility or recurrent fractures, a defect in type I collagen is unlikely.

Type IV collagen

is a major component of basement membranes, and its defects are associated with Alport syndrome, a disorder affecting the kidneys, eyes, and ears. Alport syndrome presents with progressive kidney disease, hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities, none of which are evident in this case. The patient’s symptoms, including joint hypermobility and vascular fragility, point to a defect in type III collagen rather than type IV collagen.

question:
A 24-year-old nulliparous female with a history of recurrent deep vein thrombosis presents with shortness of breath. The full blood count and clotting screen reveals the following results:


Hb	12.4 g/dl
Plt	137
WBC	7.5 * 109/l
 
PT	14 secs
APTT	46 secs

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Third generation oral contraceptive pill use
explanation:
Antiphospholipid syndrome: (paradoxically) prolonged APTT + low platelets

The correct answer is antiphospholipid syndrome. The key features in this case pointing towards antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) are the young female patient with recurrent deep vein thrombosis, mild thrombocytopenia (platelet count 137), and a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) of 46 seconds. APS is an autoimmune condition characterised by the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies which interfere with phospholipid-dependent coagulation tests, leading to a prolonged APTT. The presence of thrombocytopenia is also a common finding in APS.

Third generation oral contraceptive pill use

can indeed increase the risk of thrombosis, but would not explain the prolonged APTT or the thrombocytopenia. Additionally, the contraceptive pill would typically be discontinued after the first thrombotic event, making this an unlikely cause of recurrent thrombosis.

Protein C deficiency

is an inherited thrombophilia that can cause recurrent thrombosis, but it does not typically affect the APTT or platelet count. The coagulation screen would typically show normal PT and APTT values in protein C deficiency.

Antithrombin III deficiency

is another inherited thrombophilia that can cause recurrent thrombosis. However, like protein C deficiency, it does not typically cause prolongation of the APTT or thrombocytopenia. The coagulation parameters would usually be normal.

Activated protein C resistance

, most commonly caused by Factor V Leiden mutation, is the most common inherited thrombophilia. While it can cause recurrent thrombosis, it does not typically cause prolongation of the APTT or thrombocytopenia. In fact, activated protein C resistance typically shows a normal or shortened APTT.

question: A 47-year-old female is referred to the rheumatology clinic due to cold fingers. Which connective tissue disease is most strongly associated with Raynaud's phenomenon?
Perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA) are most strongly associated with which condition?
explanation:
cANCA = granulomatosis with polyangiitis; pANCA = eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis + others

The correct answer is

Churg-Strauss syndrome

, which shows a strong association with perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA). pANCA is particularly associated with Churg-Strauss syndrome (now known as Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis or EGPA), with approximately 40-60% of patients testing positive. The presence of pANCA in EGPA helps distinguish it from other vasculitides and is useful in diagnosis and monitoring disease activity.

Goodpasture's syndrome

is actually associated with anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies rather than pANCA. These antibodies target type IV collagen in the basement membrane of the lungs and kidneys.

Polyarteritis nodosa

is typically ANCA-negative, which helps distinguish it from other forms of systemic vasculitis. This is an important diagnostic feature of the condition.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

(formerly Wegener's granulomatosis) is strongly associated with cytoplasmic ANCA (cANCA) rather than pANCA. The target antigen is typically proteinase 3 (PR3).

Autoimmune hepatitis

, while it can be associated with various autoantibodies, is not typically associated with pANCA. The main antibodies seen in autoimmune hepatitis are anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA) and anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA).

question:
A 57-year-old man presents to his GP with right-sided hip stiffness and difficulty mobilising. He reports no history of trauma. Although he has no significant past medical history, he discloses that he has been consuming approximately 750ml of vodka daily for the past 10 years.

On examination, there is pain and a reduced range of movement in all directions of the right hip, while the left side remains unaffected.

What is the best imaging modality to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
MRI is the investigation of choice for avascular necrosis of the hip

The patient has presented with unilateral right-sided hip pain and restricted movement. When considered alongside the patient's history of chronic alcohol abuse, these symptoms are highly indicative of avascular necrosis of the hip. While plain radiographs may be utilised as an initial investigative tool, they frequently appear normal in early stages and therefore are not the optimal modality for confirming this diagnosis.

MRI

is recognised as the superior imaging technique for establishing a diagnosis of avascular necrosis of the hip.

CT

scans are not routinely employed to diagnose avascular necrosis of the hip due to their inferior accuracy when compared to MRI. Although CT can provide more intricate images of complex fractures that may be useful pre-operatively, there is no reported trauma in this case to suggest that a fracture has occurred. Should a fracture be suspected, an x-ray would typically serve as the primary investigation.

DEXA

scanning is instrumental in measuring bone mineral density and diagnosing conditions such as osteopenia and osteoporosis, but it is not utilised for detecting avascular necrosis of the hip, which remains our primary concern in this scenario. Osteoporosis usually presents without symptoms yet heightens the risk of fragility fractures. Nevertheless, without any history of trauma, a fracture remains improbable.

Radionuclide bone scans

require administering a small quantity of radioactive isotope that emits gamma rays detectable through analysis. This isotopic uptake occurs at specific sites, including malignancies; however, such scans are not routinely conducted for avascular necrosis of the hip since MRI has proven more sensitive for diagnostic purposes.

An

X-ray

might typically be ordered initially but often yields normal results, particularly in early disease stages. An MRI's greater sensitivity makes it the preferred imaging modality under these circumstances.

question:
A 33-year-old female presents with pain and stiffness in her right knee, which she's had for the last 3 months. On further questioning, she also has pain and stiffness in her left wrist and the distal interphalangeal joint of her right index finger. Her symptoms are worse in the morning and seem to improve throughout the day. She reports that her late mother also had joint problems; but does not know the diagnosis, although she recalls that her fingers were completely swollen before she started treatment.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Inflammatory arthritis involving DIP swelling and dactylitis points to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis

Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy, that most commonly presents as an oligoarthritis (usually involving fewer than 3 joints for the first 6 months ). It can involve any joint in the body, but unlike rheumatoid arthritis often affects the distal interphalangeal joints. Other common symptoms of psoriatic arthritis included dactylitis 'sausage digit', inflammation of an entire digit and nail changes such as onycholysis. In 15-20% of cases, symptoms of arthritis are detected before psoriasis appears.

Rheumatoid arthritis typically presents as a symmetrical polyarthritis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease which has a wide range of clinical and laboratory features which can be remembered using the pneumonic 'SOAP BRAIN MD'.

'SOAP BRAIN MD'

Serositis: pleurisy or pericarditis
Oral ulcers
Arthritis
Photosensitivity

Blood: anaemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia
Renal disorder: lupus nephritis - minimal mesangial, mesangial proliferative, focal, diffuse, membranous and advanced sclerosis
Antinuclear antibody
Immunology: anti-Smith, anti-ds DNA and antiphospholipid antibody
Neurologic disorder: seizures or psychosis

Malar rash
Discoid rash

Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome), is inflammatory arthritis that develops in response to an infection. The classic triad of symptoms is inflammatory arthritis of large joints, inflammation of the eyes (conjunctivitis or uveitis), and urethritis/cervicitis.

Reactive arthritis: conjunctivitis/uveitis, urethritis/cervicitis and arthritis 'can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'

Gonococcal arthritis is a single or multiple joint septic arthritis caused by disseminated gonococcal infection.

question:
A 22-year-old man with Sephardic Jewish ancestry presents with severe abdominal pain of several hours' duration. He has associated nausea but no constipation. He has a history of similar episodes and recurrent febrile illnesses in the past, which usually last 2 or 3 days. He reports these episodes first started around the age of 13.

On examination, his temperature is currently 39.2ºC. He has generalised, severe abdominal tenderness with guarding. Bowel sounds are present. Given the likely diagnosis, the patient is given colchicine.

What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
explanation:
Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal recessive, hereditary inflammatory disorder characterised by reoccurring episodes of abdominal pain, fever, arthralgia, and chest pain

The condition in the scenario above is familial Mediterranean fever (FMF), given the recurrent episodes of abdominal pain with associated fever. Treatment with colchicine is another clue to the diagnosis. The correct answer regarding inheritance is autosomal recessive. The condition is more commonly seen in people of Mediterranean or Arab origin.

The other modes of inheritance are therefore incorrect - FMF is an autosomal recessive disorder.

question: A 54-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a history of right shoulder pain. On examination there is limited movement of the right shoulder in all directions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for developing adhesive capsulitis

Adhesive capsulitis

is strongly associated with diabetes and classically presents with global restriction of both active and passive movement, often described by patients as a ‘frozen’ shoulder. External rotation is usually the first and most markedly affected movement. Pain may predominate early (the freezing phase) before stiffness becomes the principal complaint (adhesive phase). The loss of passive range distinguishes it from many other shoulder pathologies, and the examination finding of limitation in all directions – as in this vignette – is highly characteristic. Imaging is frequently normal, so the diagnosis is predominantly clinical, and recognising the association with diabetes is key.

Rotator cuff tendinopathy

typically causes painful restriction of active abduction and elevation, but passive range remains relatively preserved because the joint capsule is uninvolved. Patients often describe a painful arc between 60–120° of abduction rather than the global stiffness seen here. Hence, although common, it does not fully account for limitation in every plane.

Avascular necrosis

of the humeral head can lead to pain and progressive stiffness, yet it is far less common, usually linked to chronic corticosteroid use, alcohol excess, sickle-cell disease or prior trauma. Radiographs or MRI usually reveal subchondral collapse or a crescent sign, features not hinted at in this scenario, making it a less likely single best answer.

Diabetic amyotrophy

causes asymmetric proximal motor neuropathy affecting the thigh girdle far more than the upper limb. When shoulder girdle involvement occurs, weakness rather than capsular stiffness predominates, and passive motion should remain full. Consequently, it does not fit the examination finding of restricted passive range in all directions.

Glenohumeral osteoarthritis

can mimic frozen shoulder with pain and stiffness, but it is uncommon before the age of 60 and usually follows significant trauma, chronic rotator cuff disease or inflammatory arthropathy. Crepitus, joint line tenderness and radiographic evidence of joint space narrowing and osteophytes help differentiate it. In a 54-year-old diabetic without trauma or crepitus, adhesive capsulitis remains the most likely diagnosis.

question:
A 50-year-old woman is brought in to the GP by her concerned son. The patient has established mental health issues meaning she rarely leaves home however she is able to carry out activities of daily life unaided.

Her son is concerned as over the past several months the patient has reported increased generalised joint and bone pain, particularly affecting the spine and legs, with associated general weakness. On examination, she has long bone tenderness, weakness of the proximal muscles and difficulty walking with a 'waddling gait'.

Based on the patient's presentation what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bone pain, tenderness and proximal myopathy (→ waddling gait) → ?osteomalacia

This patient has presented with joint and bone pain, tenderness, and evidence of proximal myopathy in the form of a waddling gait, all suggestive of

osteomalacia

. With the patient rarely leaving home she is at risk of a lack of sunlight and therefore vitamin D deficiency. This vitamin D deficiency results in decreased bone mineralisation and softening of the bone. Unlikely other bone pathologies, patients with osteomalacia are not only at risk of bone fractures but also commonly experience joint and bone pain and muscle weakness especially in the form of proximal myopathy.

Osteopenia

is due to low bone density and normally precedes osteoporosis. As with osteoporosis, patients are at risk of bone fractures but the low bone mass itself does not normally cause symptoms. Pain (unless fractures are present) and weakness is not commonly associated with the condition.

Osteoporosis

is the more severe form of reduced bone mass when compared to osteopenia. As such patients are at higher risk of bone fractures however again the condition itself does not cause symptoms. Again, joint pain, proximal weakness and a waddling gait are not associated with osteoporosis.

Paget disease

is due to dysregulation of bone remodelling resulting in excessive bone breakdown and subsequent disorganised new bone formation. Although affected patients can experience bone pain, most patients are asymptomatic. The commonest features of the condition include skull frontal bossing, headaches, and hearing loss (secondary to auditory foramen narrowing). Joint pain, proximal weakness and the subsequent waddling gait are not associated with Paget disease.

Scurvy

is a result of vitamin C deficiency and therefore is rarely seen unless in cases of extreme self-neglect or alcoholism. Symptoms can include weakness and bone pain but patients will normally have skin changes, easy bruising, petechiae, poor wound healing and gum disease. There is no evidence of these features on examination nor any clear evidence of dietary deficiency making scurvy unlikely.

question: An 28-year-old man is investigated for recurrent lower back pain. A diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis is suspected. Which one of the following investigations is most useful?
explanation:
Diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis can be best supported by sacro-ilitis on a pelvic X-ray

The correct answer is X-ray of the sacro-iliac joints. Sacroiliitis is a hallmark feature of ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and is typically bilateral and symmetric. Plain radiography of the sacroiliac joints is the initial imaging modality of choice for suspected AS according to NICE guidelines. The modified New York criteria for AS diagnosis require radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis as a crucial component. Early changes include joint space irregularity and sclerosis, progressing to erosions and eventual ankylosis.

ESR

is a non-specific marker of inflammation that may be elevated in AS but is neither sensitive nor specific enough for diagnosis. Some patients with active AS may have normal ESR values, while elevated levels can occur in numerous other conditions. Therefore, while ESR is useful in monitoring disease activity, it is not the most useful diagnostic investigation.

HLA-B27 testing

, while associated with AS (present in about 90% of patients with AS), is not diagnostic. The presence of HLA-B27 alone is insufficient for diagnosis as it occurs in 8% of the general population and many HLA-B27 positive individuals never develop AS. Additionally, AS can occur in HLA-B27 negative individuals.

X-ray of the thoracic spine

is less useful than sacroiliac imaging in early disease. While thoracic spine changes (such as squaring of vertebrae and syndesmophytes) do occur in AS, these typically develop later in the disease course and are not as helpful for initial diagnosis.

CT of the lumbar spine

is not the first-line imaging investigation for suspected AS. While CT provides detailed bony anatomy, it involves higher radiation exposure and is generally reserved for cases where radiographs are inconclusive or when complications are suspected. MRI would be more appropriate than CT if advanced imaging is required, particularly for detecting early inflammatory changes.

question:
A 53-year-old woman is referred to a general medicine clinic following a low-trauma fracture. The patient reports suffering a femoral neck fracture after falling over whilst playing tennis. She was diagnosed with coeliac disease whilst in hospital receiving treatment for her fracture. Otherwise, she has no other significant medical history.

Her blood tests are as follows:


Calcium	2.01 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Phosphate	0.67 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)
Magnesium	0.9 mmol/L	(0.7-1.0)


Bilirubin	15 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	140 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	11 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	12 u/L	(8 - 60)

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Low serum calcium, low serum phosphate, raised ALP and raised PTH - osteomalacia

Osteomalacia

is the correct answer. Osteomalacia results in low serum calcium, low serum phosphate and a raised ALP, as seen in this patient. Osteomalacia is most commonly caused by vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D deficiency can be caused by coeliac disease, which this patient has been recently diagnosed with. Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin - its absorption from the gastrointestinal tract relies on fat absorption, which is impaired in coeliac disease. Osteomalacia results in lower mineral content of bones (with excess uncalcified osteoid and cartilage), resulting in more fragile bones that are more prone to fractures.

Hypoparathyroidism

is the incorrect answer. Hypoparathyroidism will result in low serum calcium and therefore cause bones that are more prone to fractures. However, hypoparathyroidism would cause a high serum phosphate and it would not affect ALP levels.

Osteoporosis

is the incorrect answer. Osteoporosis causes reduced bone density, increasing the chance of fractures. However, osteoporosis does not affect serum calcium or phosphate levels and does not affect ALP.

Paget's disease

is the incorrect answer. Paget's disease results in focal areas of increased bone remodelling, resulting in overgrowth of poorly organised bone - this leads to deformities and increases the risk of fractures. However, Paget's disease does not affect serum calcium or phosphate levels. It normally causes a significant rise in ALP.

Renal failure

is the incorrect answer. Chronic kidney disease / renal failure is associated with bone disease that can increase the risk of fractures. This is a multifactorial process.
